To investigate the risks of overfitting in co-learning schemes for Schrödinger eigenvalue problems with high dimensions, we examine the generalization capacity of two-layer neural networks using minimal data sets and assess the corresponding estimation errors. By employing the double-sided co-learning approach, we explore the impact of network size and data quantity on the network's generalization capability in one-dimensional hydrogen atom cases, and the results show that network size and data quantity can significantly influence the generalization capacity. Furthermore, we observe that generalization errors decrease as the basis function degree increases for different networks, and we observe the phenomenon of "saturated generalization capacity."

The origins of the most energetic particles from the universe, called ultra-high-energy cosmic rays, and the source of the particles with the highest energy, have still not been identified. The extreme anisotropy in the direction of these particles, observed at energies greater than 4 EeV, may provide a vital clue. The anomalous anisotropy pattern, consisting of an excess in the southern hemisphere and elongated structures, has been detected since 2004 by the Pierre Auger Observatory. The statistical significance of the excess, when analyzed with data up to 2013, was found to be at 7.8 sigma, and when further analyzed with additional data, the significance increased significantly. The most recent analysis, incorporating four years of operational data, showed that the anisotropy in the direction of these particles is highly significant at energies greater than 4 EeV, with a statistical significance of 13 sigma. The most energetic particles, with energies exceeding 8 EeV, showed no significant anisotropy, with a statistical significance of 2.6 sigma. The anisotropy in the direction of these particles, with energies between 16 and 56 EeV, was found to be significant at 3.4 sigma. The statistical significance was determined using a likelihood analysis and was found to be robust against changes in the modeling, and the systematic uncertainty was found to be smaller than the statistical uncertainty.

Homogenization was utilized to analyze thin films in a commensurate approximate state within the framework of an energy model featuring H1 gradients.
The resulting homogenized energy demonstrated local minimization properties in the L1 space.
Similar investigations into thin films in discommensurate approximations within a 3D Ising-type energy model resulted in minimal L1 homogenized energies.
Here, a similar approach to homogenization is used with a specific energy model for thin films with gradients in W2,k spaces, exhibiting non-linear elasticity.
The homogenized energy was found to be locally minimizable in Lk+1 spaces.

Starting with a straightforward Lagrangian for a self-interacting Dirac field within a curved spacetime, we derive the corresponding Hamiltonian and canonical equations of motion, first assuming a (3+1)-dimensional curved space and general metric. Applying this framework to the complex Dirac field in a curved spacetime, we obtain a set of coupled equations for the interacting Dirac fields when the spacetime is described by the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker metric.

Training a deep learning model to categorize tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in histopathology images is challenging due to limited data sets, making it difficult to create a model that can accurately identify lymphocytes within complex tissue environments. This problem can be addressed by leveraging federated learning, which enables multiple institutions to collaboratively train a model without sharing sensitive patient data. A prototype of federated learning has been developed and tested with a multi-site data set of colorectal cancer images, showing that this technique can effectively combine expertise from multiple sources to create a accurate model for tumor infiltration assessment.

Cavity magnomechanics offers a unique opportunity to develop complex quantum systems with significant technological potential. A newly proposed system utilizes a free-electron laser connected to a magnetic free-standing 2D material, consisting of two parallel plates, within a high-Q optical cavity. The magnon-photon coupling between the system and the cavity exhibits strong behavior under specific conditions, enabling direct access to magnon-photon state characteristics. Our research demonstrates the application of two protocols for producing quantum states at these interfaces, comprising the stimulated swing protocol and a modified version known as the swing protocol with two pulses. The stimulated swing protocol relies on an additional control drive to switch magnon and photon populations, while allowing for stabilization of the photons. The modified swing protocol utilizes a second control cavity to produce swing-like movements in the magnon-photon space, combined with rapid pulse applications to generate quantum entanglement at these interfaces, thereby outperforming stimulated swing in terms of entanglement production.

Our research introduces a novel reinforcement learning method combined with a trusted evolutionary algorithm to automatically create trajectories for a quadrupedal robot, learning its movements without manual intervention. This innovative approach fusion enables real-time planning and execution of a quadrupedal robot's movements on challenging terrains. By testing this strategy on a simulated model and a physical robot based on Intel's Dextr technology, we demonstrate its efficiency in navigating complex landscapes. Furthermore, our results show that this strategy can be applied to a wide range of quadrupedal robots.

The low-luminosity active galaxy in low-ionization nuclear emission-line region is an enigmatic phenomenon.  High-resolution X-ray spectroscopy of NGC 7213, a prototypical LLAGN, was conducted using the XMM-Newton and Chandra observatories.  Although this source lacks an obvious broad iron emission line, our analysis detected significant ionized gas moving at approximately 400-500 km per second.  Specifically, the Fe XXV and Fe XXVI emission lines at 6.67 and 6.97 Angstroms were identified in the soft X-ray band, whereas the O VII, O VIII, and Ne IX emission lines fell within the ultraviolet range.  Furthermore, the Fe XXV and Fe XXVI emission lines were found to be asymmetric, with the maximum iron emission intensity occurring on the red side.  Based on our observations, the hot plasma in this low-luminosity active galaxy is moving at approximately 600 km per second, in accordance with previous studies of similar sources.  Therefore, this data indicates that the supermassive black hole in this low-luminosity active galaxy is moving at approximately 600 km per speed, with further research required to determine the exact origin of this hot wind.

A novel reconfiguration approach based on reinforcement learning is proposed for the model-free optimal control of a nonlinear system. The new strategy combines elements of the optimal linear regulator, reinforcement learning, and a nonlinear feedback mechanism. By integrating these components, a more robust and adaptive control solution is achieved. The proposed method utilizes a simplified model of the linear optimal regulator, which depends only on a pre-computed gain matrix. Through a nonlinear transformation, this gain is applied to the original coordinates, enabling a quick and efficient control application with minimal computational overhead. The original coordinates are updated in a model-free reinforcement learning process, allowing the originally optimal linear controller to adapt to changes in the system's nominal conditions and maintain optimal performance in a nominal configuration. The proposed approach demonstrates robustness during reconfiguration and parameter tuning, and enables the maintenance of optimal performance through reconfiguration. The strategy was successfully applied to the optimal and robust control of a non-linear optical table, achieving significant reductions in position variance due to external disturbances.

The SiD detector, a key component of the Future Circular Collider (FCC), is designed to provide comprehensive coverage of particles created in high-energy particle collisions. With a radial depth of approximately 14 meters and significant levels of particle radiation, the SiD detector requires a robust and innovative design. To address these challenges, we propose a new concept for the SiD's innermost components, featuring a radiation-resistant silicon vertex detector with a carbon fiber structure. We also introduce a innovative design for the electron calorimeter, utilizing a forward placement and a new material composition. In addition, we explore solutions for the detector's tracking and calorimetry systems in the presence of significant magnetic fields. These solutions aim to optimize the detector's performance, even in difficult conditions, such as those caused by a strong 16 Tesla magnetic field. Our study demonstrates the feasibility of this detector design, which has the potential to uncover groundbreaking discoveries in high-energy particle physics.

We've conducted an extensive study of the densely-populated star field in the center of the galaxy CLM J092504.8+442003.1 (Tonantzintla 2), located within the cluster Virgo, using the APOGEE archive. This region is particularly significant due to the high concentration of ancient globular clusters and numerous massive dwarf spheroidal galaxies. By analyzing the stellar velocities, we found that the core of this ancient star cluster exhibits a relatively low surface brightness profile with a half-light radius of 0.44 kpc. This profile indicates that the majority of its stars follow a 3-dimensional Gaussian distribution. Based on our color-magnitude diagram analysis, the cluster's main sequence turnoff stars display minimal metallicity and abundance variation, while its red giant branch stars show a narrower metallicity range but larger abundance variations. These metallicity and abundance values, however, do not indicate any distinct population within the cluster. Tonantzintla 2 has a relatively bright absolute magnitude for a cluster, with a M_F425W of -7.36. This high luminosity is unusual for a cluster and is not consistent with its properties. This could be due to the presence of a blue horizontal branch, but our data does not support this hypothesis. Earth-observing satellites are becoming increasingly popular for training Machine Learning models, but existing datasets are limited in size and quality. To address this issue, a new resource has been developed to enhance AI applications in planet observation. This resource, known as EarthNets, consists of a comprehensive collection of 31 publicly available datasets in the remote sensing domain, each meticulously annotated and balanced. By providing detailed information about the geospatial location, spatial scale, and imaging technology for every sample, EarthNets enables researchers to analyze and replicate the performance of various deep learning models across a wide range of realistic earth-observation scenarios. Our analysis reveals significant performance disparities between models when tested under different settings, and EarthNets can be utilized to evaluate the resilience of existing image analysis methods when environmental conditions change. Furthermore, the resource supports researchers in exploring potential biases in their models and helps them establish baseline performance levels for various earth-observation tasks.

A novel approach to form a hydrodynamic theory for active nematics in any spatial dimension is developed, which enables comparison with existing models and derivation of a new theory for 2D active nematics. Utilizing dynamic renormalization group methods, it's discovered that nonlocal stress closure and Gaussian fluctuations are significant in 2D active nematics and lead to altered behavior and modified physical parameters. However, these effects are subleading in dimensions greater than 2.

Reading articles in foreign languages is often hindered by irregular spelling patterns that vary by region or country.  Current detection methods are insufficient due to their over-reliance on fixed rules and inability to handle diverse patterns effectively.  To address this issue, a new detection framework called ReAD has been developed.  By breaking down text into potential regionally irregular words using a dynamic partition approach, the framework enhances detection accuracy and adaptability across various contexts and setups.  Moreover, a detailed analysis of the detection problem has been undertaken to create effective detection models capable of identifying regional spelling inconsistencies.  Experimental results using a newly created dataset showcasing European spelling variations demonstrate a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing methods, with notable gains observed in real-world applications such as detecting German spelling changes from KiKi to LiLi.

In a recent study utilizing lattice QCKT data with fine lattices and precise simulations, key data points are analyzed to understand the low energy behavior of two-point correlation functions. As a result, important data on the hadronic contribution to the muon's flavor-dependent anomaly, particularly $(g-2)$, have been determined. Specifically, constraints are placed on the first zero of the pion vector form factor, with an estimated value of $Q_{\pi} < 1440$ MeV. Furthermore, hadronic contributions were calculated, amounting to $(64 \pm 4)$ (GeV)$^2$ and $(642 \pm 10)$ (GeV)$^2$ for the light and strange quark electrics, respectively. These contributions are then compared to experimental data, particularly for the muon's flavor-dependent anomaly, $(g-2)$.

A new approach to code analysis called Global Representation for Code (ReCo) is proposed to address the limitations of existing methods that focus on local properties of lines or statements and fail to capture code structure effectively. Our innovative method transforms various code elements into a unified, multi-dimensional space, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of code structure. Using ReCo as a foundation, a novel line-of-code dependency analysis model is developed, outperforming the traditional single-pair comparison approach in empirical tests. Our method also facilitates the detection of code dependencies across different languages, making it a versatile tool for code understanding. Our findings are further validated by using ReCo for a comprehensive analysis of the evolution of projects over time, uncovering additional dependencies that were missed by previous methods.

Using a comprehensive galaxy sample from the CANDELS dataset, we have calculated stellar masses for over 100,000 galaxies and combined these with previously published halo masses for the same objects. The resulting data reveal a unique relationship between a galaxy's mass and its morphological type. Specifically, in certain mass ranges, we've discovered that lighter galaxies are more likely to take on a spiral shape, whereas heavier galaxies are more likely to be elliptical. The transition point, where light distribution correlates with mass, shifts depending on mass. For lighter galaxies, this transition occurs at lower mass, while for heavier galaxies, it occurs at higher mass. This supports the hypothesis that more massive galaxies require more time to transform into heavy, elliptical-shaped halo masses.

A straightforward and inexpensive method using stellar brightness to measure interplanetary dust is effective in estimating global aerosol properties. However, individual estimates come with large uncertainties due to assumptions about the distribution of light from different wavelengths. These assumptions have hindered the accuracy of connecting local measurements by radar and radiance to the overall state of space dust. We tested a new light model based on past research and our own data to see if it improves estimation accuracy. By applying this new model to a data set, we achieved better results and connected the measurements in the process. Our analysis also revealed that using standard light assumptions can lead to errors in calculating the energy transfer between particles of different sizes. We anticipate that these improvements will enable a better connection between various global light measurements.

The GGLlasso Python package implements a generalized graphically structured sparse regression model, initially described in the research by Taylor et al. (2010). A key feature of this model is its ability to identify groups of variables that are represented by predefined designs, which can be uniform or non-uniform. The objective of this model is to find a balance between predicting a response variable and maintaining groups of graphs with shared edge sparsity levels, which is controlled by a specific tuning parameter. The adjustment of this parameter along with the overall scaling factor can significantly impact the detected graph structure. To address this challenge, researchers have developed a new method that automatically determines these two parameters using a stable version of the model. The solution provided by this method serves as the basis for all other tuning parameter values and is selected based on its proximity to the model's input graphs. The gglasso function in the GGLlasso Python package implements this optimized method and is supported by a set of tools for visualizing the resulting graphs and correlations between variable sets.

High-resolution radio observations of developing disks have the potential to distinguish between two models of substantial mass loss: one based on the evaporation of disks facilitated by extreme ultraviolet radiation, and another depicting mass loss driven by magnetohydrodynamic disk winds. By accurately measuring mass loss rates and radial extents of disk winds at various frequency bands, future observations from facilities like the ALMA and submillimeter ATLAS could confirm which model accurately describes the phenomenon observed in the disk around the young star, TW Hydrae. Our research demonstrates that photoevaporation and MHD disk wind models produce distinct radio signatures due to differences in outflow velocity and disk structure. While both models generate mass loss rates comparable to those measured in other young stars, they differ significantly in radio emission patterns. An observation at 87 micro meters would likely fall within the radius margin of a MHD disk wind model, and mass loss occurring at frequencies lower than 87 micro meters could be attributed either to the peripheral escape of disk material or to mass loss driven by two distinct models.

A system has been created that combines speech segmentation, speech classification and acoustic modelling into a unified framework. The speech signal is viewed as a sequence of features whose values change over time, and an unsupervised algorithm based on a hidden Markov model is used to categorize the speech signal. The model identifies the speech and unvoiced regions, and then a more refined model is developed to estimate a sequence of fundamental frequency values. The model can also automatically select the optimal number of speech source states, and the need for training data can be minimized by using a simplified model before the main model is created. The performance of the model has been evaluated and the results show that the model can perform well with a level of accuracy comparable to that of systems using trained acoustic models.

A new variant of the Inertial Forward-Reverse Backtracking algorithm is presented, which effectively solves symmetric variational inequalities and other related problems such as optimization and min-max problems. Notably, this algorithm, based on the reverse Banach fixed point method, showcases nearly linear convergence under the strong monotonicity assumption and, even in the absence of this assumption, achieves an almost linearly convergent rate by incorporating a dynamical damping mechanism for numerical stability. The performance of this algorithm was empirically validated through thorough numerical experiments.

This research investigates the impact of loop corrections on Higgs particle masses within a modified supersymmetric model, specifically incorporating a mechanism for generating neutrino masses. By utilizing the Feynmann diagrams, we demonstrate that these loop corrections significantly contribute to neutrino masses and are consistent with the predicted neutrino mass range, without fine-tuning. The findings also demonstrate that loop corrections to Higgs particle masses significantly improve their predictions, aligning with the predicted mass of 125 GeV. Furthermore, we examine the effects of these loop corrections on the relationship between Higgs coupling and the Standard Model.

The Neural Architecture Search (NAS) problem can be approached in two primary ways: by optimizing the hyperparameters of a predefined network structure or by automatically discovering the optimal architecture itself. A significant limitation of current optimization-based methods is their substantial computational requirements. On the other hand, a large body of research has focused on heuristic or evolutionary approaches, but these often involve time-consuming manual adjustments of the search space. Moreover, a vast number of possible architectures have remained untapped. To address this, a novel method is proposed that draws from sequence-based architecture search techniques, aiming to synthesize more efficient network architectures for specific deep learning tasks. The proposed method involves a search for more efficient alternatives to well-known architectures, like ResNet-52, by optimizing their properties such as the number of filters in each layer. The results show that significant computational speedups of up to 2.4x are achieved with the synthesized architectures, while often matching the accuracy of the original ResNet models. The code for this method is publicly available on GitHub.

In the future of wireless communication, millimeter wave (mmWave) multi-group multicasting is set to become a key technology for serving numerous users with limited hardware. However, due to its limited range and blocky signals, mmWave has high vulnerability to user mobility and signal obstruction. This paper explores a novel method to enhance mmWave's reliability by combining it with sub-radio frequency, leveraging a dual-band access point to provide different frequencies for different groups of users. A new hybrid encoding technique is proposed to streamline the hardware needed to switch between these frequencies and automatically adjust mmWave's beamforming without prior knowledge of user positions. Through simulations, this method shows a notable improvement in signal packet delivery success rates compared to mmWave alone, demonstrating a substantial increase in the number of successfully received packets.

A new approach to the secure multi-party computation problem, called federated extraction (FE), presents an attractive alternative. In FE, multiple parties jointly calculate a secret function without ever exchanging data. Although related to the well-known federated learning framework, FE differs in that no learning occurs and a single output is produced. We propose a novel communication-efficient Federated Extraction (FE) scheme, where a specific function $f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ is determined by secret inputs $x_1,\ldots,x_n$. The communication complexity of our scheme is $O(\max_{i\in [1,n]} |x_i|)$, which contrasts with existing methods requiring $O(n\cdot \max_{i\in [1,n]} |x_i|)$, thereby eliminating an unnecessary $n$-fold increase in communication.

In the future's smart environment, Named Data Networking (NDN) is expected to connect to a virtual layer of edge computing, forming an integrated framework that combines data retrieval and Edge Cloud resources. This integration presents complex management challenges, particularly in coordinating the DNN and computing layers to achieve optimal performance. A key goal is to maximize data transfer rates and minimize end-to-end delay. This study addresses a dynamic coordination issue, where an intelligent DNN router distributes requests across multiple edge servers, simultaneously deciding on data replication patterns and request routing. A Markov Decision Process (MDP) model is created for this purpose, and an optimal policy is found using backward induction. To apply this solution in real-world scenarios, where multiple data layers and extensive state spaces are involved, a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) method is proposed as an efficient approximation. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through simulations in simulated C++ networks, compared with traditional routing methods.

We've established that under specific conditions, an Euler-Bernoulli beam extending across a star-shaped graph remains stable when equipped with damping. It's discovered that the spectrum of the associated linear system is empty, leading to the conclusion that only certain combinations of damping along one arm and boundary conditions are capable of ensuring both asymptotic and exponential stability.

In the quark-meson model incorporating explicit chiral symmetry breaking, a significant inflection point is encountered when a constant external inflexion density surpasses a certain threshold. This critical inflection density inflexion is directly proportional to the magnitude of the external inflexion density, with the proportionality constant being the critical mass of the pion. Beyond this threshold, the system enters a complex state, exhibiting multiple domains with distinct orientations, each aligned in different directions. The inflection domain wall separating these domains exhibits a pattern reminiscent of the caustic structure, with its geometry determined by the relative pressures of the quarks and the external inflexion density.

To effectively utilize prior knowledge in multi-objective (MO) genetic algorithm parameter optimization, we propose two methods, namely, utility function learning with one objective and robust utility function learning with three objectives. Both frameworks enable the incorporation of one or more objectives when forming the utility function. The proposed utility functions are constructed using support vector regression, a machine learning technique, and are found to enhance convergence speed when supported by prior information. The proposed utility functions are observed to outperform a Pareto utility function in scenarios involving three objectives and simultaneous incorporation of multiple objectives, while showing comparable performance in situations with only one objective.

In response to growing concerns about the security of machine learning systems, researchers have established a framework for adversarial attacks that could be executed by human operators or automated tools. This framework has led to the development of multiple attack strategies, with a focus on minimal perturbations or label misclassifications. However, most existing research has focused on image classification attacks, leaving relatively little knowledge about the vulnerability of autonomous agents in dynamic environments. To bridge this knowledge gap, this study presents two black-box attacks on reinforcement learning agents that could be implemented without prior knowledge about the target policy or the environment. These attacks, named RIP (Reward-Importance Perturbation) and ARI (Action-Representation Injection), aim to maximize the impact on the target policy's reward while requiring only limited modifications to the test environment. RIP achieves this by approximating the time derivative of the reward using a single-step perturbation, whereas ARI exploits the linear properties of feed-forward neural networks to generate a misleading representation of the environment and induce abnormal actions. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of these attacks in both 2D and 3D scenarios, with significant reductions in the target policy's reward.

The application of external influences, such as external fields or vertical distortions, in a 2D phosphorene model can effectively eliminate symmetry-breaking vertical distortions, thus removing the phosphorene's non-symmetry characteristics. This elimination allows for the tunability of the phosphorene's Dirac points. Our research has found that when external influences, such as electric fields, are applied, a specific external field threshold is needed to restore the lattice symmetry, thus allowing for the non-symmetry of the phosphorene's band structure. When this threshold is exceeded, the Dirac points shift, thus allowing for the creation of a 2D material that can exist in both symmetry and non-symmetry states.

In a non-stationary Markov decision process, we investigate the optimal strategy in a risk-sensitive setting. The optimal strategy's quality is closely tied to the "Dynamic Regret" over multiple time periods. We establish a lower bound for this regret and prove that our previously developed risk-sensitive learning algorithm achieves the same level of performance. As the time interval increases, we show that identifying the best policy becomes easier. Additionally, we demonstrate that over extended periods, we can effectively isolate non-stationary components and achieve near-optimal performance by adjusting our confidence levels for exploration.

The effectiveness of issue tracking software in software development projects is widely acknowledged. The popular bug-tracking service Jira is utilized for a vast number of projects worldwide, encompassing both open-source and commercial endeavors. The project issue data hosted on Jira can offer valuable insights into software development processes; however, direct access to this data is hindered due to confidentiality and security considerations. To overcome this limitation, our study involved acquiring and making publicly available issue data from accessible Jira projects. The obtained dataset contains a total of 183,516 issues across 33 project repositories. The analysis of this dataset led to the discovery of distinct patterns in issue data and comparison of these patterns with previously published results. The outcomes of this study indicate that issue data patterns are universally applicable and not merely coincidental.

Decentralized machine learning is a key component of the federated learning paradigm, where a remote server coordinates a network of machines. Each machine performs local computations on its own data and sends updated model parameters to the server in an iterative process. To synchronize models across the network, the server combines multiple parameter vectors into a single aggregate, typically using well-known techniques. However, our research introduces a new class of aggregation functions, expanding upon existing methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by successfully aggregating deep neural network parameters in various distributed settings.

A recent breakthrough utilizes advanced integrated photonics toUltra-cold atoms. Rapidly evolving miniaturization techniques for Raman, Bragg, and Faraday gratings now allow for the implementation of complex, multi-trap systems suitable for intricate state preparation protocols. In this work, we demonstrate a novel integrated photonic structure featuring a Raman, a U-shaped Penning, a traceability laser, and a diffraction efficiency measurement grating, all fabricated on a chip. The system's uniform design simplifies operation by using a single CO2 laser source. The findings have paved the way for the development of complex atom-photon quantum circuits within a compact and highly functional integrated photonic platform.

The set of all finite, non-empty words with letters from a partially ordered set is denoted as $\Lambda^{\ast}$. Given a subset of words, we define the pre-order of inclusion to determine whether one word can be transformed into another by reordering its letters according to the specified order. This pre-order becomes a partial order when restricted to irreducible words. The resulting structure, known as the MacNeille completion of $\Lambda^{\ast}$, is built upon this partial order and consists of a collection of ideal-based subsets of words. These ideals satisfy a property in which the intersection of two ideals is equal to the set of all finite words resulting from combining subsets from each ideal. This paper presents a characterization of ideals that result from completing the partial order defined on $\Lambda^{\ast}$ with respect to a strict total order. It also establishes equivalence between this synthesis and another equivalence already in existence.

A novel computational approach combining linear regression and integer programming is presented, which enables the deduction of a polymer's chemical composition from its mass spectrometry spectrum. While mass spectrometry can provide the mass of certain components of the polymer, it cannot precisely determine their identity. Consequently, identifying these components is crucial for interpreting mass spectrometry data. By integrating linear regression and integer programming, our proposed method resolves this issue and outperforms existing solutions, which rely on less accurate heuristics. Our approach surpasses the performance of the current best-in-class method, which alone in its field has enabled polymers to be utilized in a variety of applications including diagnosing diseases, analyzing metabolic processes, detecting toxins and drugs, and forensics.

A pressing challenge in treating severe COVID-19 patients is the struggle between their high oxygen needs and limited ventilator capabilities. The problem lies in the fact that one patient can only be effectively supported by one ventilator, which limits the ability to manage multiple critically ill patients. To overcome this limitation, a technique called dual-patient ventilation has emerged, allowing two patients to be ventilated simultaneously using a single machine. To optimize this approach, a mathematical optimization method, direct transcription, has been employed to develop a viable strategy. The application of this technique is exemplified in a comprehensive case study that examines the complexities and requirements of dual-patient ventilation.

For a specific type of rational map, we prove that it has only a limited number of outcomes for its repeated transformations, in terms of topological similarity, and also establish the maximum number of distinct groups of these outcomes.

We demonstrate the validity of specific empirical Bayesian methods in predicting the parameters in these dimensions, particularly in the absence of information about the surrounding matrix's identity. We also investigate the implications of this distribution on predictive performance and its comparison to alternative methods in terms of the predictive error.
