Achieving dynamic control over line ripples in nonuniform magnetic fields is a major challenge due to their transverse polarization. The newly developed dual metasurface, incorporating split ring resonators and elliptical resonators, overcomes this limitation by converting line ripples into spinning ripples via coupled resonances. The fundamental mechanism behind this transformation can be attributed to the coupling between magnetic and electric Fock states, facilitated by anisotropic polarization conversion at the metasurface. The generated optical spin Hall effect and customizable spin orientation are also demonstrated using the proposed methodology. The proposed optical spin Hall effect and customizable spin orientation are also shown to be achievable with the assistance of computational tools. The achievable spin orientation can be adjusted by modifying geometric parameters, such as ring dimensions and material properties. The experimental setup validates the simulation results by measuring the transmission spectra and 2D maps of the transmission coefficients for different input polarizations, thus confirming the practical applicability of the concept in optical devices.

Over the last 15 years, research on collaborative learning between humans and robots has made notable advancements. However, this research remains largely confined within university settings, largely due to concerns about security, portability, and scalability. Developing open-source software frameworks, combined with advanced technologies such as the Docker container system and the TensorFlow Tensorflow, holds the potential to transform these learning systems into deployable software applications, suitable for real-world use cases like intelligent tutoring systems, online courses, and the management of extensive multi-agent environments. This study showcases the potential of using these technologies to create high-level cognitive systems through examples of human-robot collaborative learning, including the acquisition of knowledge by robots and a range of learning algorithms used in both robotic and educational applications.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation of a distribution, specifically its variance-like measurement. This measurement is particularly interested in the mean absolute deviation from the median. A specific bias-corrected estimator based on the sample has been bias-corrected. Consistent with the bias correction, the convergent rate of the bias-corrected estimator was found to be $N^{-5/4}$ both for the mean absolute deviation and for the estimator itself. In contrast, the convergent rate of the initial biased estimator was found to be $N^{-3/2}$. Although the bias of the bias-corrected estimator is confirmed to be of a higher order, specifically $O(N^{-3/2})$, it has been found that the mean absolute deviation has an optimal non-asymptotic approximation with the precision $O(N^{-3/2})$. Additionally, it has been proven that this approximation is unique. Furthermore, this precision also applies to the mean absolute deviation. Interestingly, the bias of the squared deviation from the sample median is found to be negligible at an optimal rate. Additionally, it has been proven that the bias-corrected estimator of the squared deviation is the minimal mean L1-invariant alternative with the minimum mean square error. Lastly, the performance of the bias-corrected estimators was tested through numerical experiments.

A new approach to enhancing open information extraction through knowledge graph completion has been proposed and implemented. By identifying missing relationships between key entities in a knowledge graph, the system can establish new connections between entities in text documents. This technique was used to build an annotated dataset and **InfoNLL**, an information extraction and linking library, which enables researchers to test its effectiveness in improving the accuracy of extracted relationships from text.

The impact of anisotropic momentum and finite baryonic chemical potential on U(1) phase in quarkonia J/ψ is investigated using the real-time formalism within a N-dimensional space with oblate or prolate anisotropy. By calculating color screening effects through the quasi-particle Debye mass in real time, we analyze how these factors affect quarkonia mass shifts in prolate and oblate orientations. By comparing our results with isotropic momentum cases at zero baryonic chemical potential, we identify the critical prolate or oblate anomalous mass shift point for each N-dimensional baryonic chemical potential. Additionally, we determine the prolate and oblate critical temperature (T_c) for various prolate and oblate anomalous mass shift points in N-dimensional space with finite baryonic chemical potential.

We conducted a study on the magnetic arrangement of Tb3RuO7 using neutron diffraction techniques. The research revealed that it shares structural similarities with rare-earth triflates, comprising Ru3O7 backbones consisting of alternating bond Ru chains. The effect of an internal magnetic field on the behavior of spin-3/2 Ru ions was explored through this study. The internal field arises from the influence of neighboring Tb ions, whose 7 research states cause anisotropy along the c-axis. The magnetic configuration of Tb3RuO7 consists of alternating in-plane and out-of-plane components of Tb ions M_s, applying different single anisotropy fields on adjacent Ru ions. The internal field's dependence on M_s, combined with the spin anisotropy of Ru, led to a magnetically disordered behavior. Notably, it was observed in Tb3RuO7 that a partially disordered state occurs at 1.8 K, characterized by a short-range magnetic arrangement of Ru ions within an 8 Å cubic volume.

Although explaining decisions made by deep neural networks is crucial for understanding their behavior, the validity of these explanations has been challenging due to the lack of alignment between artificial and natural vision. Our proposed method, Modulated Periodic Activations (MPA), generates periodic patterns that, when combined with a neural network, highlight the areas of an input image most influential in its classification. By adjusting the phase and wavelength of these patterns, we can produce varied visualizations without over-reliance on specific training data, thus generalizing the explanation process. We observe that MPA not only captures local aspects of decision-making but also provides a more balanced representation of global semantics compared to other visualization techniques, as shown through case studies and quantitative assessments.

In a wide array of practical applications, making predictions based on diverse populations often proves challenging. This research examines the problem of predicting labels in the presence of varied data distributions, taking into account both unbiased and biased features. Traditional adjustment methods, like domain adaptation, rely solely on unbiased features, but take little account of the rest of the data. However, this approach can be problematic when features are diverse and complex. To rectify this, we introduce semi-generative modeling, a novel method that generates data for features not considered during adjustment by conditioning on observed variables only. This enables better utilization of all features without introducing spurious correlations typical in generative models. We demonstrate that semi-generative modeling achieves better results than a standard generative model in experiments conducted under both synthetic and real-world conditions.

The primary goal of deep learning is to create intelligent systems capable of
forming abstract representations of data, which then enables them to make precise
predictions. Recent research highlights a key factor in this process: the use of
stochastic gradient descent to optimize model parameters. Despite its importance,
understanding how RL operates remains an area of active research due to DP's complex
nature. In an effort to clarify this, we will examine the representation learning
process in terms of both its inductive biases and geometric properties, ultimately
identifying commonalities with reinforcement learning.

In the context of the 3-dimensional 42 coset lattice, the influence of key elements on lattice minima is analyzed. Annewar and Scharf's discovery that the golden ratio φ influences these minima is validated. Additionally, the set of minimal vectors in this lattice is identified, and the concept of reduced binary quadratic forms is employed to establish the set's size.

In particle physics, jetting, which involves combining multiple particles, is a crucial process, and interpreting ML-based jet taggers, which use particle-level information, can be challenging. A novel approach is proposed to make jet taggers interpretable by incorporating expert-derived variables in early network layers and applying a relevance analysis technique called Layerwise Relevance Analysis to identify relevant features throughout the network. Results using this method on a particle-jet tagger for identifying Higgs bosons show that approximately 60% of the tagger's performance can be replicated using only a few particles and their associated expert variables.

For positive integer r, we examine two types of Stirling numbers: the second kind and the first kind. These numbers relate to partitions of a set and to merging two partitions into one. Specific cases of these numbers relate to Bell numbers, factorials, and Srinivasan numbers. We define new versions of these numbers, called degenerate r-related Stirling numbers, which relate to degenerate versions of Bell numbers and Srinivasan numbers. These new numbers have formulas for calculation and recurrence relations.

In crystallography, "coloring" a space group involves replacing its point group elements with matrices of arbitrary dimension. This results in "colored" space group representations that can be used to model electronic states or elastic vibrations. These states can be either single ordinary space group induced (SSGI) or double ordinary space group induced (DSGI), or they can be single/double gray strata group induced (SSGI/DSGI). Our study is on the little group irreducible representations (LIR) of these induced types. In particular, we have calculated LIR for single/double gray strata group induced types in 3888 three-dimensional space groups.

The definition of the momentum operator for the harmonic oscillator in terms of its raising and lowering operators is explored through the use of its Killing vector field integration and application of the Heisenberg picture in the harmonic oscillator system. Similar investigations are conducted using the 2D harmonic oscillator system on a cylinder or as the superposition of a 1D harmonic oscillator with a free particle, both involving the use of their respective Killing vector fields.

Quantum many-body systems experiencing non-zero spin or particle hopping in the presence of a magnetic field encounter a substantial computational obstacle due to the sign problem, with affected wave functions exhibiting complex values. To address this limitation, researchers propose employing complex-valued neural networks as a wave function ansatz, with the potential to eliminate the need for approximating wave functions with real values. However, a comprehensive examination of this proposal is still lacking in the current literature. This study delves into replacing occupied orbitals with complex-valued machine-learned wave functions, specifically by training a neural network on a model Hubbard system that exhibits minimal sign problem. Our findings indicate that training with complex values from the beginning yields unambiguous results, free of noise, even for highly correlated Hubbard models near half-filling. Notably, these results can be achieved without access to exact solutions.

A new approach to understanding composite Higgs models is developed by incorporating global symmetry breaking patterns to derive theoretical predictions for key parameters within the models. By introducing the concept of flavon fields, the method provides a systematic way to analyze the holographic parameters that result from the global symmetry breaking. The study specifically applies it to SO(6)/SO(5) and SO(10)/SO(6) × U(1) models, and the findings demonstrate that the method can make precise predictions for key parameter values within these composite Higgs models. The research also extends to a theoretical framework based on supersymmetric SO(10) geometry, where global symmetry breaking patterns give rise to multiple flavon-Higgs composite models with distinct extra U(1) symmetries. The study examines the implications of these models and their relation to the fine-tuning issue, and the findings suggest that certain models may require minimal fine-tuning to be consistent at the electroweak scale.

In virtual environments, objects often appear smaller and farther away than they really are, due to the way humans perceive depth. This visual distortion, which is more pronounced when viewing objects at a distance, has significant implications for how we interact with VR. Although the distortion is more of a curiosity at normal reading distances, it becomes overwhelming when trying to navigate large-scale VR worlds. This issue stems from the limitations of current head-mounted displays, which have low resolution, resulting in reduced frame rates and a noticeable drop in frame rate quality. This problem is particularly apparent when navigating large-scale VR environments, where the distortion would render navigation nearly impossible.

To effectively utilize large language models in various applications, it is essential to be familiar with multiple languages. The framework's success relies heavily on being trained with data from multiple languages, which leads to being proficient with the languages it has been taught. Nevertheless, this method has a limitation, as it cannot be applied to newly learned languages that have not been included in the training process. To address this issue, we have developed an approach to adapt a pre-trained multilingual model to a new language using limited resources, including less structured data. This method involves a two-stage fine-tuning process, incorporating a pre-training step with an unsupervised, pre-language modeling task. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to 11 diverse languages and comparing its performance to that of zero-shot settings. Additionally, we have successfully achieved a remarkable 17.5% improvement in the model's overall accuracy on a benchmark dataset for information extraction.

When a rotating core breaks apart, it can form multiple stellar objects.
These stellar objects have their own maximum mass, which is called the binary creation mass.
This maximum mass is around 2-3 times the mass of the sun.
Factors that influence this maximum mass include core rotation, core mass, and core temperature.
This study uses a series of simulations to determine the conditions under which cores can form binary systems.
These conditions are core mass, core rotation, core angular velocity, and core size.
Core mass determines whether core fragmentation occurs at all.
Core rotation, core angular velocity, and core size all influence the formation of stars from fragments.
These factors can lead to the formation of stars with masses as low as the sun or as high as 80 times the mass of the sun.
The mass of stars formed from fragments is around 70% of the mass of their parent core.
This is lower than the mass of stars formed through disk fragmentation, which is around 80% of the mass of their parent core.
This suggests that binary systems are likely to have lower masses than single stars, which has implications for the formation of stars through fragmentation.

This research introduces M-ar-Kanonical Fast Independent Vector Analysis in a specific context. We propose two related approaches: one utilizes a multilinear tensor to represent data dynamics across multiple domains, while the other employs an autoencoder architecture for learning these dynamics. Our methods achieve improvements over traditional IVDAs by reducing dimensionality and computational requirements, all while maintaining the core principles of existing methods. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed multilinear approach in the analysis of video sequences and the effectiveness of our autoencoder-based method when applied to visual features for anomaly detection tasks.

The equivalence between two theorems has long been regarded as the most compelling argument for the connection between finite model theory and polynomial calculus. However, a new research paper challenges this perspective by demonstrating that this connection is tenuous. Specifically, the paper shows that while extended polynomial calculus can tell apart certain types of graphs – such as bipartite versus non-bipartite – in a relatively straightforward manner, similar distinctions take exponentially more effort when using polynomial calculus.

The given text presents original findings related to a specific type of noncommutative algebra, which is an elementary algebra denoted as $\sigma$. The study builds upon existing research, particularly a significant discovery made by Masiambo et al in 2019, which identified finite rings with specific properties based on the prime number 3. The current research expands on this finding, demonstrating the existence of an infinite supply of $\sigma$-elementary rings, each sized according to any given prime number. Additionally, the findings related to $\sigma$- elementary rings, which were initially discovered by Parmenter in 1979, are connected. Specifically, the research shows that a specific property, related to a prime number, exists in a simplified, standardized form within the context of $\sigma$-noncommutative algebra.

We are particularly interested in identifying the conditions under which a certain type of function, known as Unfalsifiable Claims, fails to hold within a given framework of properties for sets or relations. Our research focuses on establishing a framework of categories based on the computational complexity of this process. First, we demonstrate that determining when Unfalsifiable Claims fail has a decidable computational complexity. Next, we introduce a method for organizing properties into distinct classes, defined by their relationship to decidable computational complexity, and then we show that these classes are closed under various operations. Finally, we draw a comparison with the Tarski-Bergman hierarchy, highlighting the similarities and differences between them.

A significant number of traffic accidents and congestion events are initiated by specific incidents such as vehicle malfunctions, collisions, or poor road conditions. Timely identification of these incidents is crucial for effective traffic management and road safety. This study focuses on using spatio-temporal patterns in social media posts with location data to identify traffic accidents and congestion in real-time. The discovered incident times are then compared to traditional detection methods using sensor data to assess the effectiveness of this new approach. The analysis reveals that social media data can accurately detect incidents and estimate recovery times, providing valuable insights for real-time traffic monitoring and management.

A new method has been developed to compute the cosmic microwave background's primordial non-Gaussianity parameter $f_{NL}^{non-G}$ by analyzing the bispectrum of the combined cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure. An approximate non-Gaussian signal is estimated by combining large-scale structure data with the lensing effect of the cosmic microwave background, which is then used to extract the non-Gaussian signal from a combination of these datasets. This approach allows researchers to not only study the non-Gaussian signal but also to investigate long-wavelength short-range correlations. Assuming that instrumental noise can be minimized to a certain level, the forecasted detection limit for the non-Gaussianity parameter $f_{NL}$ is approximately 3.4 using current data from the Planck satellite and eBOSS dataset.

By integrating concepts from Bayesian inference and adversarial robustness,
we establish a novel framework that enables accurate predictions of test data,
even under challenging conditions.
Our approach is theoretically grounded, and we empirically validate its effectiveness under various forms of distribution shift.
We achieve this by introducing an novel objective function that encourages predictions to be both uncertain and confident.
This framework enables trained models to not only express uncertainty but also quantify adaptability when faced with unfamiliar data.
We further provide a new decision-making tool for situations where trained models may encounter unfamiliar data.
This framework enables trained models to adapt to new data by utilizing posterior expectations.

Online rumors spread rapidly during the COVID-19 pandemic in China, leading to the development of a model that analyzes both the temporal patterns of rumor propagation and its underlying driving forces. This model, which is applied to a dataset of Chinese online rumors, enables both supervised and unsupervised force-directed force-directed influence measurement of online rumors. By combining this analysis with a new method for detecting peak propagation times, a new approach for identifying driving forces has been developed. These driving forces are found to include fear, curiosity, and the pursuit of benefits, while it was also observed that top Chinese influencers play a significant role in accelerating the spread of rumors. Ultimately, it was discovered that false rumors tend to be more influential than true ones.

In hyperspectral classification tasks, the complexity of spectral features poses significant challenges. Recent research has shown that the linear model's efficacy is constrained by the intrinsic dimensionality of data, which itself is influenced by spectral dimensionality. As spectral dimensionality surpasses a critical threshold, known as the spectral phase transition, it negatively impacts classification accuracy. This study delves into the relationship between spectral and spatial dimensions, demonstrating that spectral dimensionality not only affects individual pixel performance but also has implications for entire spectral images. Furthermore, the study evaluates the classification outcomes of various methods applied to the Pavia University image, all of which suffer from the phase transition phenomenon. To mitigate this issue, the study proposes an approach to reduce spectral dimensionality, thereby enhancing classification accuracy and potentially simplifying linear models for hyperspectral data analysis.

Recent advancements in language models have been significant, but they come with a drawback - a large size. A solution to this issue would greatly improve their environmental impact and deployability. A new framework has been developed to compress any language model by a large margin, with an average compression rate of 40%, while retaining 98% of their original performance. This method is versatile and can be applied to any model architecture without relying on specific characteristics, with a time complexity of linear proportion to the training time. As a result, achieving compressed models is comparable to achieving a standard trained model. A demonstration of its effectiveness is shown with an Annotated Therapeutic Interaction model trained from scratch using the proposed compression framework.

A novel method is proposed that employs ab initio quantum mechanics to calculate the hydrogen-bonded amide proton chemical shifts for a protein in order to facilitate structure validation and refinement. By integrating these shifts with existing NMR data, the method can accurately determine protein structures. Our approach involves calculating the shifts for a 14-residue peptide, HCWKAPQICTCYKAA, using the ABACUS code, in agreement with prior research. Furthermore, the calculated hydrogen-bonded amide proton chemical shifts demonstrate considerable correlation with experimental data. Structure determination for the peptide was achieved by combining our calculated values with existing NMR data. The results show that our method can effectively guide protein structure optimization and account for local environmental effects.

Deep learning models rely heavily on choosing the right loss function for their training, which significantly impacts their final performance. Despite being widely used in applications like computer vision and NLP, there isn't enough research exploring how loss function variations affect training. A systematic investigation is needed to understand the consequences of swapping loss functions for specific tasks. This study focuses on examining how swapping CNN-based models' loss functions influences their training outcomes. By conducting experiments with six different CNN architectures and 11 distinct loss functions on three distinct image classification datasets, we discovered significant variations in the resulting models' accuracy. Notably, replacing the standard Cross-Entropy loss with an alternative, the Multi-Class Focal Loss, yielded better results on harder images, like those in the INRIA dataset. Our findings also highlight the importance of training robust models for complex data by using MCFL, which outperformed traditional CE in handling harder data points. Overall, our research emphasizes the need for carefully evaluating loss function impacts when choosing a primary function for a task.

We've developed a novel Hamiltonian perspective on the parquet theory by combining the constrained and the restricted restricted matrices as its fundamental components. The new formulation seamlessly integrates the various self-energies and susceptibility in the parquet theory's solution framework. Additionally, the proposed Hamiltonian exhibits symmetry for the S matrix under particle-hole and particle-particle exchanges.

Utilizing the constrained local density approximation, a groundbreaking ab initio
method has been developed to calculate exciton condensation, enabling the theoretical
prediction of phase diagrams. This innovative technique has successfully led to the
theoretical discovery of exciton insulator phases in monolayer and double-layer
exciton condensates. Additionally, the method has been used to investigate the nature
of exciton condensation in monolayer TiSe2. Our findings reveal that exciton condensation
in TiSe2 is not driven by Fermi surface nesting but is rather a correlation effect.
However, the existence of a nested large hole pocket has been shown to facilitate
the formation of a exciton insulator by minimizing the ground state energy. This
research paves the way for the potential realization of exciton insulators under
excited states in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides.

A large-scale analysis of over 10,000 community safety reports submitted by the public through a text-based reporting platform and accompanied by 1,000 recorded dispatching interactions was conducted using a unique dataset and corresponding reporting system. Our study and data annotation revealed the previously unexplored dynamics between users and dispatchers within a community safety framework. We identified and categorized various types of threats, threats per type, and their associated severity levels. Furthermore, we examined user and dispatcher behaviors, including the types of threats and levels of urgency assigned to them. We found significant disparities between the perspectives of users and dispatchers, with users perceiving more property threats, but dispatchers deeming more violent threats to be urgent. We also observed variations in decision-making among dispatchers, including the assignment of 20% of all threats as not requiring attention. To promote effective human-AI systems for threat detection and urgency assignment, we proposed several guidelines based on the discovered facts and presented initial results applying a large language model in this context.

To analyze the impact of nematicity on a superconductor's magnetic response, researchers have developed a model based on a simplified two-band system where the interaction between electrons and non-spherical gap properties affects the unused band minimally, mimicking a minimal conductivity two-band system, and have calculated the magnetic response in this setup, and found that the magnetic response is influenced by an unusual ratio of conductivities in the unused band.

A key challenge in distributed machine learning from non-stationary data sources is a fundamental limitation that stops models from reaching optimal performance. A theorems has been established showing that in order to overcome this limitation, a model must be able to adapt to changes occurring at an rate proportional to the fourth root of logarithm of time. This research presents a new distributed learning method that can overcome this limitation by learning in a way that balances adapting to the present data distribution and retaining knowledge from past distributions. This adaptive approach enables the model to efficiently and effectively track the present data distribution without losing valuable information, thus achieving better results. A strong guarantee on achieving optimal performance is provided by a new upper bound on regret growth over time, showing that in order to overcome this limitation, a model must be able to achieve a regret growth of order t. This is achieved by designing a new distributed learning method based on the principle of minimax, which combines adapting to the present data distribution and retaining knowledge from past distributions. This new approach uses a weighted ensemble of past and present online learning methods to achieve better results.

The increasing difficulty in tracking down music sheet music over recent decades has made it impractical to study music using traditional methods. To overcome this challenge, we developed a method to quantify and visualize the musical styles of several prominent composers from the 20th and 21st centuries. Our research focuses on music from the following composers: Schoenberg, Berg, Webern, Bartok, Shostakovich, Penderecki, Lutoslawski, Carter, and Regeczi. To represent their music visually, we created spectrograms, which are then analyzed using advanced machine learning techniques to identify distinctive musical features. The results indicate that music from Schoenberg to Penderecki has become more complex over time, whereas the musical language of Carter and Regeczi is similar to that of Bartok, suggesting that their music may be becoming less difficult for modern musicians to learn and perform.

A novel, multi-entry reinforcement process is presented, extending the classic
one-entry reinforcement mechanisms (such as P\'{o}lya urns and random graphs) to scenarios involving multiple entry points and correlations. Our analysis reveals that, under certain conditions, the classic one-entry processes can be seen as special cases of our model. By applying a sophisticated mathematical technique, we prove that the asymptotic behavior of a broad class of additive functionals in this process converges to a specific distribution, as seen with the application of a functional central limit theorem.

Building upon the foundational concepts of Parigot's $\lambda$-calcul with modalities and Juillet's modality introduction rule, we have introduced a rule that facilitates computation at the level of modalities within the Java language. This has led to the development of a new proof theory that is orthogonal and covers full reduction in a specific context, named Computational Ludics. By integrating this theory with a visualization of proofs as interactions in a specific medium, we have reinterpreted key results in this domain. Specifically, we have redefined and proven the strong normalization and confluence of full reduction in this specific context, as well as established a cut-elimination theorem. This result demonstrates that any interaction between two well-designed strategies can be transformed into a unique interaction between their respective components.

A prominent method for learning reward functions in reinforcement learning is preference learning, which learns the agent's preferences by comparing pairs of rewarded behaviors. The difficulty lies in identifying distinct feature sets that correspond to the preference pairs. Existing research employs clustering techniques to group states, but these often overlook temporal information in actions. Furthermore, learning a cluster map requires a large number of reward pairs, which can be inefficient. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel framework that learns a time-sensitive cluster map using visual aids. By leveraging visual sensors on robots, we reduce the learning burden and define distinct areas based on visual features. A cluster ranking process is then used to learn the ordered preferences associated with each area, eliminating the need for pairwise comparisons. The proposed framework has been successfully tested on a robotic platform with multiple entities, demonstrating its effectiveness in real-world robotic applications.

We reevaluate the Smyth phase space's topological properties by examining its relationship with the Lawson monad and the interaction between upper closures in ordered spaces and Smyth embeddings. Furthermore, we identify core-compactness as a fundamental characteristic of Smyth phase spaces, leveraging which we also demonstrate that a core-compact phase space is equivalently characterized by the existence of a local basis consisting of Scott-open sets.

In a superfluid or a viscous fluid carrying a quantized vortex at a boundary in two dimensions, the angle of the vortex at the boundary is found to have a stable configuration. In the absence of viscosity, all vortices at the boundary must be acute. In a purely inviscid fluid, the steady states are only achievable at angles that are either zero or ninety degrees. Introducing viscosity allows for non-zero, non-nine-tenths-degree stable states, with the timescale for reaching this stable angle proportional to the inverse of the times the vortex velocity over the viscosity, providing evidence for a generalized surface-pinned property at the boundary.

A crucial step in causal analysis is addressing confounding biases. For observed variables, augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW) achieves this by combining an outcome regression and a propensity score. While AIPW has seen significant applications with machine learning predictions, its reliance on propensity score assumptions may still introduce considerable variance. In contrast, an alternative approach called standardized augmented inverse probability weighting (SAIPW) uses outcome regression and propensity score residualization to achieve dual robustness and potentially lower variance. However, SAIPW's application with machine learning predictions has been lacking. In this work, we develop a novel implementation of SAIPW with neural network predictions and demonstrate that it leads to more accurate estimates in certain scenarios. Additionally, to minimize the impact of overfitting on machine learning estimators, we propose using cross-fitting. Finally, we establish the asymptotic normality of SAIPW with neural network estimators and/or random forest estimators under specific conditions.

The recent discovery of tau anomaly at Belle II and other tau factory experiments has rekindled interest in exotic tau decays, which could be linked to new physics beyond the Standard Model. To effectively investigate this, a high theoretical accuracy in predicting Standard Model decays of the tau is required. This corresponds to the second term in the experimental measurement of coupling constants, which has a 0.3% value. However, achieving such a theoretical accuracy is currently a major challenge. Moreover, understanding the QCD hadronization process, which contributes to the experimental measurement, also demands precise theoretical predictions. In this talk, some of the current difficulties in theoretical predictions for tau decays will be discussed and possible solutions will be proposed to help in identifying potential new physics in upcoming data from the Belle II experiment and other facilities.

A detailed comparison of laboratory and simulation models in a rotating annulus has been conducted to study the development of atmospheric circulation systems. This is the initial comprehensive study to compare the results of an experiment using a physical model with those from a numerical simulation. Three research groups have carried out the experiment: Tuckerman et al. at Caltech in 1982, Clever et al. at the University of Oxford in 2008, and the present authors at the University of Oxford in 2015. Initially, we present Tuckerman et al.'s study and show how the data was collected, the research setup, the findings, and the methods used. Next, we compare the results of our recent research with a numerical simulation using the spectral method. This comparison reveals significant differences between the two approaches, particularly in terms of the research area size selection, the height variations, and frequency analysis of the waves. Lastly, we discuss how the various factors may have contributed to these discrepancies.

A typical approach to Bayesian inference for extreme value distributions involves maximum likelihood estimation based on threshold-exceeded exceedances, which can be reformulated as estimating a Tweedie distribution using zero-truncated Poisson data, enabling the use of standard Bayesian inference methods, including Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, within the Stan framework.

A fundamental assumption in reinforcement learning (RL) is that the training environment is consistent, an assumption which is generally not met in corrupted settings where a portion of the received rewards are randomly distorted. In light of this discrepancy, particularly considering its significance in offline RL where the agent is trained using a pre-collected dataset, there is a pressing need for developing RL algorithms that are robust to corruption in the training data. Existing solutions either require an overly strict condition on the level of data corruption or make unrealistic modifications to the problem setting. This study introduces new, more practical guarantees for reward corruption in offline RL by introducing a modified version of the problem called corrupted Markov decision processes (CMDPs), which is a more flexible framework that does not impose restrictive limitations on the distribution of corrupted data. A dynamic programming-based approach is proposed to construct a virtual environment that is consistent with the corrupted dataset, and the method has new, improved performance guarantees under less restrictive conditions on the level of data corruption. Moreover, this framework is extended to handle both symmetric and asymmetric data corruption in offline RL.

The log-convexity of solutions to the 1-D heat equation with dynamic boundary conditions has been examined under the condition of a logarithmically concave initial data. Furthermore, a control problem within this framework was considered, and sufficient conditions for approximate ergodic control were established.

A consensus has not been reached on the definition of out-of-distribution (OOD) text for natural language processing. We propose categorizing OOD into distinct classes and suggest a unified definition for a data point that deviates from the criteria established by its respective category. We also present identification methods for each class of OOD. Our study focuses on benchmarking the effectiveness of these methods in an established benchmark for out-of-distribution detection. The results indicate that an approach combining multiple OOD categories yields superior outcomes.

In the realm of single molecular electronics, the stochastic movement of a brownian rotor is governed by a series of inelastic electron tunneling events. A mathematical model describes the tunneling process as both stochastic and non-local, resulting in a coupled set of non-linear differential equations that simulate the complex interaction between the electron system and the molecular browser. By solving this model, researchers can calculate key metrics, such as the current, efficiency, and heat generation within the system. The model's solutions also allow for the analysis of several statistical properties, such as the temporal and spatial distributions of the brownian motor, as well as the power spectra of the motor's rotational motion. The mathematical model is sufficiently general to be able to describe various molecular engines, such as the junction between a CO molecule and a gold surface, and provides a theoretical framework for the design of novel single-electron devices.

A binary transducer T can be reprogrammed into an equivalent binary transducer 
T' having restricted growth, where every input string is processed in at most two 
passes through T'. It's also demonstrated that making T' grow only in one 
direction requires the length of its outputs on each pass to be limited by a 
fixed amount.

The concept of generalized convolution is an extension of traditional convolution, which takes two polynomials, four integers representing shift amounts, and calculates every possible version of the convolution with modified polynomials (shifted left by the specified amounts) and changes its sign accordingly. In this paper, a method is developed to directly calculate these versions, bypassing the need to first find the original convolution. The generalized convolution is utilized in the direct computation of multishifted polynomial evaluations and has also been used to optimize a previously proposed method for this evaluation. Furthermore, the optimization can be applied to speed up polynomial division by a single polynomial and the solution of quadratic equations, which has applications in finding roots via the quadratic formula. Specifically, the accelerated multishifted evaluation outperforms the standard Horner method by a significant factor in the number of operations required.

Recent studies have provided diverse atmospheric models for the ultra-cool dwarf GJ 229B. By using an updated version of the APOLLO model and data from the Hubble Key Program, we present a new approach. This involves combining high-resolution spectra from the VLT/VISIR instrument and lower-resolution spectra from the Keck NIRC2 instrument, which enables us to determine the atmospheric properties of GJ 229 at a temperature of 650 K. Our results show that clouds significantly impact this atmosphere, particularly in the mid-infrared spectrum, and are a major factor in the variability observed in the NIRC2 data at a 1.6 micron wavelength. Our analysis also reveals that volcanic activity on Earth-like planets could have a noticeable effect on their atmospheric temperatures and emit mid-infrared radiation, which could be detectable by future space telescopes. Our study provides valuable insights into the atmospheres of ultra-cool dwarfs and other low-mass objects, contributing to the knowledge of exoplanet and satellite atmospheric analysis.

To identify the characteristics of a recently discovered exotic state with no previously assigned characteristics, a comprehensive analysis was carried out using the framework of light cone sum rules, focusing on the possibility of it being an exotic state with a unique combination of vector vectors and a scalar, all while preserving its integrity as a nonet. Our findings indicate that this approach is effective in this context due to the absence of background issues, leading to a determined G-parity of -1 for the exotic state with a predicted mass of 4.31 GeV. The results from this study also allow for an estimation of the coupling strength between the exotic state and its corresponding meson pair, with a calculated value of 0.31, and further demonstrate the effectiveness of light cone sum rules in exploring the properties of exotic states.

My presentation will cover the latest results from the LHCb collaboration concerning the phase angle $\phi_s$ and the decay width difference $\Delta\Gamma_s$. These key parameters in the $s\rightarrow s'$ transition can be compared with theoretical predictions to test the standard model's validity. Specifically, $\phi_s$ is expected to be around -2000 micro radians and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ is anticipated to be approximately 0.15 per cent of the mass $m_s$, according to the standard model. However, current data has significant uncertainties, encompassing both the non-standard model expectations of zero for these parameters. The presentation will cover the experimental methods and analyses used to measure $\phi_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ using $s$ baryons and decays to both fully and partially differently decayed states.

On a crowded urban bus, passengers are seated in close proximity, with the driver, distinct from the average rider, moving at a slower pace. While this setting might suggest complex, variable air flow, our goal is to demonstrate the effectiveness of the well-mixed model in calculating the probability of disease transmission from an infected person to an uninfected passenger due to airborne pathogens. This model is particularly relevant given the recent cases of SARS-CoV-2 transmission that occurred in enclosed spaces. A key factor influencing infection risk is the time an individual spends on the bus. Since the time spent by the average passenger differs from the time the infected person is on the bus, we apply a mathematical approach based on the principles of the law of large numbers to infer the dynamics of the entire bus system from the perspective of an individual. This method allows us to utilize well-mixed models, which are computationally efficient, in contrast to more complex models that account for the bus's geometry and are less practical. Our analysis reveals that the stationary distribution, used in well-mixed models, can be derived from the time-averaged exposure an individual has over their bus ride. This derivation relies heavily on the ratio of the bus's length to its width, making the use of well-mixed models a viable option in such settings.

Using a shell-model approach, we've analyzed recent non- recoil-based spectroscopic data from $^{137}$Te decay. Our calculations for the beta-decay properties of $^{113-137}$Te encompass a wide range of isotopes within the Xenon region by incorporating multiple computational models: the MBPT code for the very lightest Te isotopes and the NUSHELL.MS with various model spaces for the heavier Te isotopes. Notably, including the spin-orbit term in the NUSHELL.MS calculations yielded notably better agreement with experimental data on $\log ft$ values. However, even with precise theoretical predictions, there's a noticeable discrepancy in $\log ft$ values for $^{135,137}$Te. Consequently, we propose an unconventional decay mechanism for these Te isotopes, one that could explain their unexpected large $\log ft$ values without necessitating a revision of the nuclear structure model.

Double-sided auctions serve as a fundamental exchange mechanism in various marketplaces, and a key issue arises from the double-sided nature, presenting a vital key insight as well. This work focuses on a valid double-sided auction designed for general financial markets, and it is set within a competitive framework where participants submit bids representing their personal utility functions for a particular commodity. The validated auction ensures beneficial outcomes for all participants by guaranteeing essential conditions necessary for global optimization, and it key features include global support, continuity, and differentiability. The findings encompass both mathematical proofs and numerical demonstrations, and they key include a method based on the double-sided Koml\'{o}s-Shapley theorem and an iterative optimization process. The validated auction has been tested in a simulated double-sided electricity market scenario, and it is anticipated to provide a solid foundation for other similar applications.

Using heavy quark effective theory, HQET, we examine the properties of the F-wave bottom mesons. Through HQET, the heavy and light constituent quark interaction, the light dilaton field, and the heavy quark motion are accounted for, enabling a calculation of the radial wave functions. These, in turn, facilitate the determination of the mass spectrum and the decay widths of the F-wave bottom mesons. Our analysis, utilizing HQET, yields results consistent with those obtained using lattice QCD, providing insight into the unique hadronic forces at play within these systems.

Researchers have established a connection between the underlying algebra of a finite linear automaton in direct generalization of Moore-McMillan theorem in encoding any finite automaton with a periodically structured transition decomposition. This decomposition consists of matrices that either maintain or reduce distances between elements of a metric space, analogous to the concept of homomorphisms in automata theory. Furthermore, we provide an automatic method to determine the minimum length of a nonexpansive pathway in any given automaton with a finite state set, implementing a shortening procedure for the path.

A new technique is developed to boost the accuracy of a popular data analysis
method, Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD), especially when dealing with systems
that exhibit clear patterns. To address issues related to noisy or incomplete data,
the problem of finding an optimal analysis method is reformulated as a kernel
learning problem. By utilizing the remarkable properties of kernel functions, the
new approach produces an improved DMD-like transformation that accurately
replicate the system's behavior even after being subjected to various distortions.
Notably, the novel "LANDO" algorithm not only enhances the robustness of standard
DMD but also generates highly accurate predictions for system dynamics, regardless
of whether the underlying process is linear or contains prominent nonlinear characteristics.

The widespread appeal of chess stems from its intellectual depth, with online platforms such as Lichess.org and Chess.com facilitating matches between humans and AI across varying skill levels. To better comprehend the game, particularly its opening strategies employed by players at different proficiency levels, we analyze database information from both websites. By applying concepts from information theory, specifically generalizing the H-entropy measure to multivariate systems, we establish a metric for assessing the complexity of opening play and the similarity between games. Our research specifically examines the effects of time constraints on H-entropy for games featuring popular openings, including the Ruy Lopez and the King's Pawn Game, with the latter showing nearly double the H-entropy when following an established sequence of moves compared to a more complex sequence in the Ruy Lopez.

Deriving the characteristics of cold, pale dwarf stars orbiting millisecond pulsars (MSPs) is crucial for understanding how these star pairs evolve. Although pale dwarfs are challenging to detect due to their extremely low brightness, recent advancements in detecting MSPs have enhanced our ability to identify these star pairs. This has facilitated the study of pale dwarfs that are not obscured by other stars. This research employs pale dwarfs that are believed to be part of pairs with MSRs, which were found by combining data from Chandra X-ray Telescope and Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory observations. Analysis of these observations revealed a rotational period of 3.71 days for one of the pale dwarfs, providing strong evidence that these dark objects are indeed pale dwarfs. This discovery supports theoretical predictions of pale dwarf formation and suggests a potential application of the information gained from MSRs in detecting and characterizing these dark objects.

A comprehensive theory is developed to create non-local representations of quantities of motion for an arbitrary movement under a general order Lagrangian, applicable to a wide range of scenarios including the one-dimensional dynamics of any order for both bosons and fermions, as well as $p$-dimensional fermionic systems of any order. This theory enables not only a complete description of non-local movements but also raises important questions about the extensions of Heisenberg's uncertainty principle in higher-order systems and orders of heisenberg exponents for both bosonic and fermionic cases.

Our research focuses on converting free-form 3D sketches into detailed shapes. These sketches are typically simpler and lack specific characteristics. In virtual reality, users can create more expressive designs than in traditional 2D interfaces. We've developed a system for collecting large datasets of sketches in 3D space and demonstrated its effectiveness in a drawing-based shape retrieval task. This initial dataset comprises roughly 500 entries and our results indicate that using it for learning achieves competitive accuracy compared to other methods that don't require annotated data. We've also achieved a 60% successful retrieval rate for a specific tool. To enhance our results using this domain-specific knowledge, we've created a new extension to an existing method that achieves a 70% accurate retrieval. For more information, visit the project website: http://3vrdrawing.com.

HD80606b, a hot Jupiter with a very short 11-day orbit around its host star, undergoes dramatic temperature and brightness changes as it moves from the outer reaches of its orbit back to its highly illuminated path. These extreme conditions make it an excellent candidate for various atmospheric studies with the James Webb Space Telescope. Understanding the planet's precise orbit is essential for accurately predicting its pericenter passages, which is necessary for a variety of observations. A recent study utilizing extensive transit and eclipse data from various sources, combined with transit observations made possible by the Timescape Timeshift Project, allowed for a more accurate pericenter time prediction. Accurate pericenter predictions, with margins of less than a minute for the upcoming years, will facilitate a wide range of observations, such as transit and eclipse phase curves, with various observational opportunities with JWST.

In this research, we investigate the gravitational collapse of a spherically symmetric isentropic perfect fluid and establish the feasibility of collapse with a linear equation of state, where the coefficient is negative. Our investigation reveals that this scenario is indeed possible and entropic collapse occurs under specific conditions: the entire spacetime must be of type III or a specific combination of types I and II; additionally, if the fluid belongs to a single component, the spacetime must be of type I; if the fluid consists of distinct matter and radiation, the spacetime should be a mixture of types I and II. Our findings also indicate that in entropic collapse, either the fluid belongs to Killing vector fields, or it is part of a cosmological fluid with non-constant properties. Notably, if the fluid is a cosmological fluid with constant coefficient, the spacetime belongs to type III, and if the coefficient is non-constant, the spacetime is a mixture of types I and II. Our analysis further shows that if the fluid is a Killing vector field, the spacetime belongs to type III, and if it is a non-constant vector field, the spacetime is a mixture of types I and II.

By utilizing the Iyer-Wald formalism, we've derived a corrected expression for the first law of thermodynamics in extremal black holes by analyzing the properties of an arbitrary spacetime with an extremal horizon. Using this framework, we've re-evaluated the mass and entropy of extremal black holes hawking-ing their own radiation, and found that quantum corrections significantly impact their thermodynamic behavior. Our work paves the way for exploring the thermodynamics of non-extremal black holes hawking-ing their own radiation as well.

A new framework has been developed to analyze one-dimensional motor learning tasks from the perspective of effect control. Initially, the framework utilizes an established cost function to assess performance quality, building on previous research in advanced motor control. Next, the framework examines how task effects emerge, starting with the concept of nested dynamics, where both the task and the agent's movements evolve over time. Through this lens, the framework identifies how an agent can achieve an optimal outcome by prioritizing the rate of change of an effect over the rate of change of its signal, ultimately leading to error correction. Following this, the framework explores the concept of motor synergies, arguing that skilled motor control involves generating multiple effects with a single input, as evidenced by variations in the outcomes when multiple agents perform similar movements. Finally, the framework demonstrates how this approach offers insights into developing efficient motor control strategies.

In a recent theory known as the vibrant Poincaré symmetry, we have developed a universal framework for one-dimensional models that maintain exact diffeomorphism symmetry and relate to Poincaré symmetry at a deeper level. Applying this framework, we have successfully derived the actions for a broad class of models consisting of any number of variables, including polyvector models made up of Poincaré forms, which we have shown can be minimized into standard particle models while preserving both the number of degrees of freedom and an exact diffeomorphism action. Furthermore, we have identified novel particle models that retain a diffeomorphism action, a feature we have applied to describe a new class of massless particle that preserves all Poincaré charges, all of which can be derived from polyvector models of the form $1\rightarrow N\rightarrow 1$.

Graph drawing has become a crucial area in computer science, emphasizing geometric properties of graphs as indicators of computability. This has led researchers to focus on specific properties, such as planarity and upward planarity, which have been shown to have linear-time recognition methods for general cases. However, these problems become more complex when analyzed through the lens of parameterized complexity, and this research aims to provide a comprehensive summary of current findings and theoretical assumptions regarding the parameterized complexity of upward planarity.

Effectively navigating through unfamiliar environments, such as large research campuses, demands a nuanced navigation strategy. Previous research found that agents could draw inspiration from trained memories but struggled to identify which memories were most beneficial when navigating new, unseen environments. To address this limitation, we present a novel approach called MemoNav that dynamically selects the most pertinent memories for navigation in unfamiliar settings using novel attention mechanisms. By doing so, MemoNav enables the navigation policy to focus on the most relevant memories for the current task, thereby enhancing its efficiency. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that MemoNav can significantly improve navigation performance and efficiency when using memories in unfamiliar environments, such as selecting only 20% of the memories 80% of the time, thereby validating its potential in knowledge-based navigation.

To enhance coverage and data rates within limited areas, small cells have been widely used since 4G LTE. However, they still can't meet the high-demand needs of users in places like stadiums and city centers. First introduced in 3GPP LTE-Advanced for the 4G era, the concept of Network Slicing was officially added to the 6G standard setting. By combining small cells and Network Slicing, we can create customized networks for specific high-density locations with unique requirements, effectively addressing the limitations of current small cell networks and providing a viable solution for 6G.

Over the past few years, researchers have increasingly turned their attention to applying dynamical systems theory to intricate networks, exploring how multiple interacting units within a framework influenced by external factors evolve over time. This comprehensive overview aims to be both an informative read for those new to the subject and a useful reference for experts in the field, presenting a detailed analysis of various applications and providing an in-depth examination of key concepts such as stability, multiple coexisting stable states, control methods, and the effects of network structure on stable states and complex dynamics. Furthermore, we examine the general principles underlying these theories and present a broader context for their applicability.

This study focuses on uncovering the relationship between operator growth and key concepts like information spread and energy dispersion in quantum systems. By examining specific models, we identify a shared connection to all three phenomena and suggest that exploring growth rates through quenches can reveal universal patterns. These findings suggest a way to extend the analysis to more complex interactions and non-stationary states, and we explore how the interior of holographic black holes follows similar growth trends as boundary concepts.

This research aims to clarify the state of the Hoyle state, which plays a crucial role in carbon nucleosynthesis. To achieve this goal, we employed an advanced, highly sensitive, and accurate alpha-particle tracking system called the NUSTAR, which consists of a nuclear-track detector and a time-proportional chamber with excellent resolution capabilities. To do so, we conducted an experiment consisting of the fusion of $^{12}$C and $^{12}$C nuclei, which resulted in the excited state of the $^{24}$Mg, which then undergoes decay into three alpha particles. To separate the Hoyle state direct-decay component from the non-resonant component, we used a sophisticated statistical analysis that takes into account the spatial distribution and temporal characteristics of the three alpha particles in each event. To do so, we used a highly accurate simulation code called CGM which accurately predicts alpha-particle final states in events, and we found that the experimental data is in good agreement with the theoretical predictions, and the data accurately reflects the theoretical predictions. In two-dimensional dynamic fracture, the behavior is significantly influenced by both inherent material length and time scales. Through the use of a two-dimensional dynamic fracture model that incorporates both nonlinear elasticity and inertia, the role of these characteristics is examined in the oscillatory and tip-splitting instabilities under specific loading conditions. The model reveals that the interaction between inherent material length and time scales gives rise to multiple solutions, resulting in dynamic fracture patterns such as oscillatory cracking, tip-splitting, and stable cracking under specific loads. Moreover, the type of material characteristics influences the transition between instability types and ultimately affects the crack propagation speed in various regimes.

When encoding rates approach capacity, there's often a significant gap between achieved and optimal rates in random network codes, which can be mitigated by using feedback. Similarly, in certain networks, knowing the state of some nodes via feedback allows for improved performance, particularly when high rates are involved. This can lead to a more nuanced understanding of asymptotic random coding exponents, revealing that a certain threshold rate exists beyond which state information via feedback yields a more favorable trade-off between rate and distance. Moreover, under specific conditions, this threshold rate can be determined by looking at a simplified version of the network, obtained by combining certain nodes and removing others. This concept applies to hypergraphs as well, where achieved rates exceed a certain threshold rate in random network codes, allowing for improved distance rates and potentially state-free codes with better distance rates.

A 3D attractive spin-1/2 Fermi gas exhibiting strong spin-orbit coupling is modeled on a square lattice, where we demonstrate through mean-field theory and numerical calculations that it can be depicted as a spheron topological superfluid with multiple nodes. These superfluid properties arise from a ground state that supports a non-zero Chern number, resulting in chiral edge states at the interface between solid and vacuum. This phenomenon is characteristic of topological superfluids that possess multiple energy gaps closing within the bulk. By examining the spin-orbit splitting, we find that the spin texture at the Fermi surface in these nodeless superfluid states is highly complex and combines aspects of both polar and axial characteristics.

The SEM-FACTS project, held at SemEval 2021: SEM-TAB-FACTS is a new task focused on validating information presented in tabular formats within scientific documents and locating supporting data within those documents. The project's dataset, consisting of 3338 examples across four categories – Table Entailment, Table Contradiction, Sentence Contradiction, and Sentence Entailment – involves validating statements and providing relevant evidence, either found in the same table or the surrounding text. The project's objectives and dataset were released at no cost for researchers to use, and a baseline model based on a table-aware BERT table-filling approach combined with a sentence encoder was developed and tested on the dataset to provide initial performance metrics for participating teams. The performance of this baseline model reached 70% in F1 scores for Table Contradiction and Table Entailment tasks, as well as Sentence Contradiction and Sentence Entailment tasks.

In quantum physics, the standard use of complex numbers in the $z$-plane has roots in the historical development by Parseval and Laplace in the 1800s. The need for a new method to analyze four-dimensional equations, which could provide insightful solutions, gave rise to the use of complex numbers. This work aims to clarify the fundamental role of complex numbers within quantum mechanics.

A graph's dimension is the smallest size of a set where every edge knows a different number of neighboring vertices in a given room. A "trimmed dimension" is a smaller, subset-based measurement that also tracks neighbor relationships between vertices and walls. This study explores both concepts in various graph types, such as paths, trees, and complex networks. We developed a general method to calculate these dimensions in any graph, along with specific formulas for many simple and compound structures.

These notes document my process of developing simplified, closed-form equations for ground-water circulation models. They are based on assumptions such as ground, water, and sediment densities being constant, ground slopes being gentle, and hydrodynamic pressure differences being minimal. Under these conditions, Darcy's Law remains applicable, and certain assumptions lead to a form of the one-dimensional diffusion equation for the water table. However, as noted by various scholars, this model often predicts water table evolution too quickly. These equations are then utilized to simulate water table changes during and after an earthquake-induced landslide in 2009 in Chile.

This research investigates the effectiveness of removing sulfur compounds in power plant flue gas through the use of a waste byproduct and UV radiation, operating at very low temperatures. The results demonstrate that UV light is essential for breaking down sulfur compounds, whereas ozone serves to remove them, providing insights into a more energy-efficient method for air pollution control.

To evaluate neuromorphic architectures, simulatingMemristive neurocomputing models is both critical and resource-intensive, especially for large-scale experiments, where time-consuming simulation can be particularly limiting. To speed up this process, we developed Time Division Multiplexing, a technique originally used in digital circuits that we now apply to spike-based neurocomputing models. By doing so, we significantly lowered the simulation time while maintaining the accuracy of the results. To make this approach more practical, we created a SystemC wrapper, enabling the Time Division Multiplexing model to interact with other SystemC-based components, such as neuromorphic memory and processors. As a result, we were able to demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique, obtaining a 5x speedup for a Single Input Weight Memristor (SIWM) based memristor crossbar and a 20x speedup for a larger 1024x1024 Memristor crossbar.

Predicting outcomes under uncertain conditions often poses significant challenges.
To overcome this, researchers have developed methods that quantify the level of confidence in predictions by generating prediction intervals.
However, these techniques typically assume independent observations, limiting their effectiveness in scenarios with underlying correlations.
To address this limitation, some studies attempt to model interdependencies using conditional probability distributions but this increases the complexity of models, requiring more data.
To bridge the gap between unconditional and conditional approaches, argument-based reasoning has emerged as a promising technique for making predictions under various sources of uncertainty.
We present a novel Indecision Forest algorithm that learns to make predictions with minimal assumptions about interdependent uncertainty sources, without needing additional data.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on multiple datasets, showing it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of predicting outcome ranges.

The DTW distance is commonly used in time series analysis for its ability to measure dissimilarity, despite its computational complexity of $O(AB)$; this can hinder its use in applications with large datasets. We've discovered that many elements in DTW are redundant, which led us to develop a pruned version, faster by an order of magnitude, by rapidly discarding those redundant components. We've further optimized this approach by proposing a new similarity search method that only calculates pruned DTW for potentially matching pairs, which we've implemented and tested on various datasets including 1D, 2D, and higher-dimensional series. We've observed that this new method outperforms existing techniques, providing both improved speed and search accuracy.
