In domains where safety and reliability are critical, regulatory bodies are increasingly demanding transparent reasoning behind decisions made by machines. This transparency is particularly important in high-stakes fields such as medicine, automotive technology, and other applications of artificial intelligence where decisions are automated. Although research has focused on enhancing the interpretability of machine learning models, particularly deep neural networks, these models often struggle to provide clear and understandable explanations due to their inherently complex and data-driven nature. To address this limitation, a new approach called concept analysis has emerged, which offers a more human-friendly method for analyzing decisions made by these models. Building on recent work, this concept analysis approach can explain not just decisions but also provide clear insights into how and why these models make the decisions they do. This chapter introduces an innovative method that combines the strengths of concept analysis and integer linear programming to overcome the concept analysis approach's traditional limitations related to efficiency. By demonstrating the concept of "neurons with concepts" and providing a proof-of-concept in distinguishing between cats and dogs in high-resolution images, this chapter showcases the potential of efficient and scalable decision-making analysis for complex artificial intelligence models.

Recent advancements in deep learning methods have led to the development of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), which have been successfully applied to various tasks such as node classification, community detection and graph classification. Despite their practical utility, a comprehensive understanding of the over-blurring phenomenon in GCNs remains limited. Building upon previous work, we provide in-depth insights into the over-blurring effect in GCNs, focusing on the network's generalization ability and the formation of community structures. Through analytical approaches, we demonstrate the critical role of the k-th eigenvectors of the graph's adjacency or Laplacian matrix in determining the learned community structures and classify nodes based on their generalized structures and labeling patterns.

A search for dark matter accompanying a leptonally decaying Z boson in proton-proton collisions is described. Data collected by the CMS experiment at the LHC with a total luminosity of 35.9 fb^-1 from runs at a 13 TeV energy are analyzed. An association between invisible dark matter and a visible Z boson is investigated through experiments involving mono-X signatures, where X represents a specific particle. A model involving the virtual exchange of a fermion and a scalar particle, resulting in a pair of dark matter particles and the radiative emission of a Z boson, is considered in the analysis. Data collected for three distinct Z boson mass ranges do not support the existence of dark matter within the specified parameter range and constraints have been set on the cross-sectional coupling of dark matter to the model's intermediary fermion particle.

We've developed new models for particle behavior in transverse directions within quantum field theory, relying on nonlocal interaction models that don't break the laws of special relativity. These models, which are not directly connected to parton splitting, are also not related to retarding effects, but they do describe the transfer of relativity violations above a certain energy threshold. Our analysis specifically examines the case of pions and finds that their transverse behavior is well-matched with experimental observations at various accelerator facilities, including SLAC, DESY, Brookhaven, and Fermilab, as well as with data from early-universe and late-stage supernova events.

Two space-based models, known as stocks and hangings, are presented as concepts for homogeneity in partial maps and complete partial maps between spaces, respectively. These models facilitate the characterization of homogeneity through stockings and hangings, thereby enabling the determination of which spaces satisfy these concepts. Furthermore, these models are utilized to establish the uniqueness of long colimits in the category of topological groups, which had previously been established through algebraic methods. This work builds on the previous models of coinductions and extensions known as clopenizations and uniformizations, respectively, as well as two related but distinct models for homogeneity in partial maps and complete partial maps.

Remote epitaxy is an innovative technique for forming new alloys. It bypasses existing layers and enables the creation of high-quality interfaces. This process is particularly beneficial when combining materials. In a study on a specific Heusler system, researchers discovered that remote epitaxy can occur without a buffer layer. A thin layer of graphene was used to facilitate this. This is particularly significant because it eliminates contamination risks associated with buffer layers. Moreover, remote epitaxy can be easily controlled, which isn't always possible when using buffer layers. By using Heusler compound CrMnSb on graphene/sapphire, researchers observed two distinct crystalline orientations. When no buffer layer was present, they achieved a body-centered tetragonal structure with a specific orientation. Introducing a sulfur hexaflouride treatment shifted the orientation to body-centered cubic without the buffer layer. These results demonstrate that remote epitaxy is achievable without the buffer layer, offering new possibilities in using this material system, particularly in spintronic applications.

In multivariate time series analysis, standard methods often fall short due to complex, heavy-tailed data distributions. A new class of multivariate GEDT models has been developed to address this limitation, particularly suitable for systems exhibiting long-range temporal dependencies. Within these models, we establish conditions ensuring consistent parameter estimation and precise asymptotic behavior for key model parameters, despite their interdependence and non-linear characteristics. This is achieved due to the availability of a common common random vector. Utilizing these theoretical findings, we created a novel estimation technique based on multivariate quantile processes, which we demonstrated to yield precise asymptotic results. Furthermore, we established conditions ensuring exact asymptotic behavior for key model parameters, leveraging insights from extreme value theory and the properties of multivariate regularly varying sequences. A crucial finding from our work is that the multivariate spectral measure can be consistently estimated using a multivariate thresholding approach, even when components exhibit varying degrees of long-range dependency. This measure is essential for modeling multivariate extremes, and our results show it enables accurate estimation of essential objects like the multivariate empirical spectral density and multivariate quantiles. These estimators facilitate precise inference about extreme risks, such as the probability of exceeding specified thresholds in future data. Our empirical evaluation, through both simulated and real-world data analysis, showcases the effectiveness of the proposed estimators in practice.

Recent observations from the James Webb Space Telescope have allowed us to see the distant galaxy cluster, EL Gordo (ACT-CL J0102$-$4915), in greater detail. This is the second most massive galaxy cluster found at the far-off distance of about 9.8 billion years ago. To understand the effects of the galaxy cluster on light from behind it, researchers used the JWST's near-infrared images to refine their model of the galaxy cluster. This refined model allowed them to discover a new, highly magnified star in the galaxy, DOG 4, which appears to be a red supergiant star based on its light spectrum. This type of star is very bright and emits most of its light in the visible part of the spectrum. This discovery provides important information about the galaxy's interior, including the number and size of these large stars. This discovery also shows that the galaxy's center contains many more of these large stars than we would have thought. This discovery also suggests that the galaxy's overall light from these large stars, known as the red supergiant light, is much brighter than we would have thought. A strategic partnership between a local network operator (LNO) and a leading global internet service (Google Internet Web Television), known as GUIT, aims to meet the growing demand for high-quality online viewing among consumers. The partnership involves negotiating a profit-sharing agreement based on the number of subscribers, which directly impacts the network's quality. Multiple negotiations take place to reach a mutually beneficial deal that maximizes the partnership's quality efficiency. The study finds an optimal profit-sharing contract that is supported by a corresponding quality efficiency contract.

In the first part of this research, we demonstrated that the relationship between available physical data on one hand, and the mathematical structure of Hilbert space in quantum theory on the other, is a loosely defined equivalence. This allows for the representation of all physical data within a Hilbert space. Building on this equivalence, our current findings show that it lifts to a tighter relationship at the level of differential graded categories. Specifically, we have shown that the corresponding functors preserve this equivalence. In the context of lifting, we considered a representable 2-categorical adjoint equivalence between the Hilbert space category and an appropriately set up category of observables. This led us to establish a rigorous correspondence between an object in the category of observables and a differential graded functor, along with a precise correspondence between the set of observables associated with a Hilbert space and the set of endomorphisms associated with that space.

The maximum of the scalar field's potential in $\alpha$-attractor models occurs at small values of the field within the Einstein frame. To properly investigate the models within the minimum of potential, where the field value is small, it is necessary to take into account the strong redshift associated with inflation. In the minimum of potential, the geometric terms dominate the field's evolution equation, resulting in a new class of "geometric domination" $\alpha$-attractor models. We develop a new class of $\alpha$-attractor models based on the shift symmetry, expressed in the form $V(\phi)=V_0\left[1+\frac{V_1}{\phi^2}\right]$, where $V_0$ represents a nearly constant potential and corresponds to de Sitter space, and $V_1$ represents a positive or negative offset from the potential's minimum. Depending on the value of $V_1$, the models either resemble the standard $\alpha$-attractor models with a linearly shifted scalar field or a new class of $\alpha$-attractor models with a constant, non-zero field. We derive a differential equation for the Hubble parameter during inflation, and calculate predictions for these models in terms of the spectral tilt $n_s$ and tensor-scalar ratio $r$. In our research, we demonstrated that for a quasi-Fuchsian surface group $\Gamma$, its associated maximal quasi-Fuchsian representation has a represented foliated structure at infinity with vertical components represented by simple closed curves that cannot be contracted in the respective ends. Furthermore, we examined whether this representation can be represented topologically equivalent to its end-equivalence class. If we assume small sufficient norms for a representation near a Fuchsian representation, we found that the represented foliated structure at an end with a vertical component represented by a curve $c$ exhibits a continuous deformation to a fuchsian representation, resulting in end-equivalence with its corresponding curve $c$ deformed into $c'$ within the other end of the quasi-Fuchsian structure.

This research establishes a connection between the cross-sectional structure of portfolio
return Alphas and the equilibrium behavior of return betas and idiosyncratic errors
in a market with diverse investor types, each driven by distinct objectives. Through
the identification of a novel class of factors, known as dynamic and state-dependent
illiquidity factors, the study provides an explanation for the sources of abnormal
return betas, which traditional models struggle to account for. Consequently, the theory
enables improved allocations of capital across sectors and sectors within industries,
when applied to markets such as equity and real estate.

Heart sound signal characteristics are significantly altered by various factors including environmental noise and medical instruments.  In order to accurately diagnose cardiovascular conditions, it is essential to analyze modified heart sounds.  Current methods for heart sound classification have focused on detecting abnormalities in ideal conditions.  We have developed a novel approach to heart sound classification that accounts for noise and medical instrument interference.  This approach involves using a multi-scale convolutional neural network to classify heart sounds in real-time, even in the presence of multiple types of interference.  We tested our method using a dataset containing 12 classes of heart sound signals and found it outperformed existing methods by an average margin of 7.5% in overall accuracy.

The "Cs+He" study has demonstrated that the Cowan et al. (2009) analysis is flawed in estimating Z exchange contributions, leading to an incorrect new physics limit. In exchange for this, the authors propose an alternative approach that also considers the $^{87}$Rb + $^{40}$Ar experiment, which yielded complementary results in addressing a similar issue.

A twist operator, one loop around a spacetime cylinder or sphere, is key to understanding the topological phase. In this research, we examine how twist operators transform under 2D space time symmetries, also known as 2D crystallographic point groups, where they acquire phase factors. For a cylinder, the point group acts by rotating both spatial and temporal dimensions, resulting in four possible phases: $(\pm 1, \pm 1)$. Our analysis reveals that these phases are constrained by physical requirements, specifically that the square of the twist operator should be equivalent to the transfer operator, which corresponds to a $2\pi$ rotation in internal space, limiting the possible phases to $(\pm 1, \pm 1)$. We then systematically classify twist operators with these properties for each of the 17 2D space groups, finding that the allowed phases depend on the specific space group, and that there are twist operators invariant under some point group actions, while others have distinct phases under others. Our research has implications for 2D topological orders and the behavior of twist operators under symmetries, particularly in chiral topological orders where the spatial and temporal rotations have opposite effects.

A theoretical model is developed to examine the relationship between cooperative climate actions and individual self-interest using the framework of public goods games. By analyzing how climate benefits are distributed across different groups with varying levels of dependence on the climate, the model reveals how these groups perceive the climate as a private good with inelastic supply or an indivisible good. Groups that are heavily affected by the climate may view it as inelastic, but this perception can be misleading as the climate's inelasticity only applies at low levels of provision, after which elasticity kicks in, leading to further environmental degradation. Through numerical simulations, the study explores how cooperative climate agreements can emerge in a world characterized by private goods, the presence of "free riders," and an ultimately elastic climate. The results show that climate pacts can be beneficial, particularly for groups less dependent on the climate, and that their formation can foster positive externalities, encouraging other groups to also participate.

This paper presents computer-implementable formulas to convert infinite series of operators into operators that act on a specific type of function space. Specifically, it manipulates a class of space-valued functions with the properties of H^+ fractional space. The study extends existing work by Douglas and Hartman, as well as the authors' previous research on 2-valued function spaces, to a more general setting. To ensure the validity of its results, the paper relies on key principles from the L^2 theory of Wiener algebra, particularly the properties of H^+ space, which are due to Hirschman and Riesz.

A recent study found that humans often deviate from standard economic predictions when bidding in second-price auctions, typically underbidding their true valuation. Researchers sought to investigate whether these discrepancies could be attributed to systematic mistakes or biased preferences, such as an excess of risk aversion. In an experiment involving 242 participants who participated in multiple rounds of second-price auctions, participants demonstrated an average bid significantly lower than their true valuation, specifically around 77% of the true value. Notably, participants tended to bid closer to their true value as the number of auctions they participated in increased, suggesting that bidding behavior may be influenced by an accumulation of experience over time.

The disparity between general relativity's equivalence principle and equivalent metrics in modified theories of gravity, such as $f(Q)$-gravity, raises questions about modified gravity's theoretical framework. To resolve this discrepancy and better understand our universe, we explore the behavior of matter-filled Bianchi-I cosmos within this theoretical framework. By examining the universe's evolution from an initial state of chaos to order, we aim to uncover how cosmos becomes isotropic. Our analysis focuses on the isotropization index and energy density, allowing us to draw conclusions about the behavior of different types of $f(Q)$-gravity, including those denoted by $\alpha Q+\beta \sqrt{\frac{Q}{2}}$, $\alpha Q+\beta \chi^2$, and $\alpha Q+\beta \sqrt{\frac{\chi^2}{2}}$, where the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ parameters define the theory. Our results show that all models exhibit isotropization due to the positive and decreasing behavior of the isotropization index in the past, provided the energy density decreases over time, thus validating the suitability of this theory for studying the universe's behavior.

We provide a specific combinatorial class of ideals comprising linear polynomials
that exhibit multiple desirable characteristics. These ideals possess factory
decompositions which facilitate the visualization of quotient Grassmannians as
composites of projective spaces through projections based on a total order scheme.
By determining a basis for these ideals with a factory structure, we analyze the
dimension and coordinate ring properties of particular Hessenberg varieties in
various settings. Using a variant of Schenck's result combined with power properties
of the coordinate rings, we demonstrate that in certain cases of characteristic p,
their coordinate rings are Frobenius split.

Neural Painters are advanced models that create paintings based on existing artistic styles, which have been surprisingly effective paintings on their own, delving into the nuances of human creativity. Neural Painters can generate continuous style transformations, showcasing two distinct transformation patterns - circular and spiral styles - when creating styles based on famous painters like Picasso and Van Gogh. This new model also provides a unique platform for exploring the pleasures of artificial creativity.

The presence of new physics at the TeV scale is strongly suggested by experimental anomalies observed in certain decays of beauty and bottomless mesons, specifically $B_{(s)}\to \phi l^+l^-$ and $B_{(s)}\to \phi\nu\bar{\nu}$ reactions. These anomalies can be explained by the presence of vector particles, potentially indicating that these particles are a result of a more fundamental, hidden structure within the force carriers of the Standard Model, like photon and Z bosons, at high energy levels, despite not being found in other searches for the new physics. This internal structure, or compositeness, can exist independently of the new heavy particles, potentially influencing the forces between fermions in new ways, like changing the force between muons and electrons, not seen in the expected patterns.

Recent datasets allowing answers to be found within documents have significantly boosted NLP models' performance on document-question answering tasks. Nonetheless, these datasets are insufficient in exploring how researchers utilize documents to acquire new knowledge, leading to documents being overused in such tasks. In contrast, researchers typically engage with documents in the following ways: they extract existing knowledge, identify gaps in understanding, and propose possible areas for exploration. Current datasets do not adequately reflect these nuances, leading to a limited exploration of how researchers process and learn from documents. In response, we present a new dataset consisting of questions and answers rooted in research papers, covering all three levels of knowledge exploration. Furthermore, we conduct an in-depth analysis of paper-based knowledge exploration from multiple angles and compare the characteristics of questions across these different levels, shedding light on potential applications in natural language processing.

In the intense environment of a collapsing massive star, neutrinos may become unstable and cluster together, potentially altering their typical long-distance behavior.  In 3-D simulations, this can lead to a sustained and growing instability that influences a supernova explosion.  However, the specifics of this process are poorly understood in complex conditions such as those found in the r-process.  This study uses fast neutrino flavor transformation simulations within 3-D models to core-collapse supernovae to gain new insights into how these transformations occur in such environments, including the development of a new fast instability in a high-Z r-rich region. Additionally, it is discovered that turbulent convection may cause the disappearance of an established fast instability, leading to a re-emergence later on, and potentially producing multiple, distinct oscillation modes, with one mode exhibiting step-like spectral features.

ADHD is a widely recognized neurodevelopmental disorder that affects children globally, and advances in neuroimaging have enabled researchers to image the human brain, providing insights into its complex structure. Analyzing the functional brain network, which connects different brain regions, is a primary area of study in understanding ADHD. To diagnose the disorder, our team has been seeking more accurate and efficient methods. By combining deep learning, which can automatically extract relevant features, with traditional machine learning, we have developed a novel approach to diagnose ADHD. By identifying key regions in resting-state fMRI data of typically developing children, our model can identify connections that are crucial for distinguishing between ADHD and normal brains. Evaluating our method across multiple datasets, we found that it outperforms current ADHD diagnosis methods, and by limiting the network to essential regions, we found that our approach still achieved superior results.

In recent years, the spread of misinformation during crisis situations like pandemics has become a significant concern. To address this issue effectively, targeted message campaigns are essential. A new mathematical model was developed to measure the impact of official messages from institutions, such as governments, on the spread of false information. The SISI discrete-time model describes the transitions between four distinct states: those who do not believe in the outbreak, those who do, those who are officially informed, and those who are not. The model considers the impact of institutions' messages in an official and unofficial context, as well as how people lose influence over time. A non-standard finite difference method was used to analyze the model's stability, ultimately revealing the conditions under which official messages can effectively control the spread of false information.

Technical documents, particularly in the engineering domain, heavily utilize domain-specific jargon in the form of acronyms. This creates challenges for document understanding when readers lack knowledge of the specific acronyms used and their corresponding full forms. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a web-based tool called MadDog, which automatically generates natural language inference rules from annotated documents to deduce the identities and expansions of acronyms present in new target documents. This innovative approach enables accurate predictions regarding the acronyms present in a target document along with their respective full forms, thereby facilitating document inference without prior knowledge of the acronyms involved. This novel technique is demonstrated to outperform existing state-of-the-art acronym identification and disambiguation methods when applied to the IEEE acronym corpus dataset. In addition to demonstrating its effectiveness, we showcase MadDog's utility by applying it to the IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control document, thereby providing up-to-date information regarding the acronyms present within that document.

In quantum Hall bar configurations with multiple terminals, our research shows that interference effects play a significant role in determining the symmetry of thermal transport properties. As a result, we can switch on and off the thermoelectric effect and related energy conversion efficiency by manipulating interference through magnetic field adjustments or temperature variations. Furthermore, we find that interplay between interference and electron-phonon interactions enables the possibility of rectifying energy flow, with higher efficiencies compared to systems unaffected by such interactions. Notably, we demonstrate that the optimal energy flow can be achieved by fine-tuning the phase-shifting properties of quantum Hall edges. The proposed phenomena can potentially be observed in experimental settings using GaAs or graphene platforms.

Our new DNA storage system achieves close to optimal space efficiency when representing data structures with or without hierarchical relationships by as much as two times. It also efficiently handles data updates in mutable datasets with hierarchical organization. The system's performance is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and is expected to be applicable in scenarios involving large, hierarchical datasets in DNA-based databases.

Two-dimensional systems in momentum space exhibit a distinct plane known as the nodal plane. When extended to three dimensions, the nodal plane develops into a closed surface or nodal loop in the momentum space. Topologically, the various configurations of the closed surface or nodal loop correspond to distinct constant properties. This is exemplified by a type of topological constant that can be calculated using the Green's function, which describes the excitations of the system. By employing the method of saddle point approximation to the Green's function, one can derive an expression for the topological constant that corresponds to a simpler model. This simplifies the calculation and provides a clear connection to the nodal surface's geometry. Furthermore, the topological constant can be expressed as an integral over the nodal loop, which connects it to experimental observables, such as those measured in the Kennedy lattice and other systems. This understanding has led to a comprehensive theory that encompasses various excitations of the system, such as phonons and photons, and exemplars such as the Kennedy lattice and other systems.

In various fields such as neuroscience and cardiology, it is common for a network of excitable cells to be dominated by a single pacemaker rhythm. Our research focuses on making precise predictions about the speed of waves generated by these pacemakers in one-dimensional arrangements of overexcited cells. The pacemaker frequency is the key factor influencing pacemaker pacing speed (PPS). We have developed analytical models for both slow and fast pacing regimes. Our findings in the fast pacing regime agree with previous simulations. However, in the slow pacing regime, our analysis reveals a previously unexplored connection between the pacemaker frequency and PPS. Specifically, our predictions suggest that PPS is proportional to the pacemaker frequency times the square root of the diffusive coefficient divided by the period of the pacemaker oscillations. In a cardiology context, our findings also show that PPS can be positively correlated with the pacemaker frequency. Our approach uses asymptotic analysis to study a simplified model known as the FitzHugh-Nagumo system.

A new, comprehensive approach is proposed for estimating a quantum system's density matrix with guaranteed accuracy in the trace norm, utilizing a sample complexity of $\tilde{\Theta}(k^2)$. It's also proven that this sample complexity is the most efficient possible. This novel algorithm's efficiency enables applications in estimating a quantum system's von Neumann entropy with error at a specific statistical level in order $\tilde{\Theta}(k^2)$. Furthermore, this new technique has implications for analyzing the unitary two-design property in systems with a specific number of qubits, leading to simplified proofs for existing results and the resolution of an old conjecture, as well as the derivation of new lower bounds. This new estimate of density matrix estimation also finds uses in analyzing the efficiency of quantum state learning in specific scenarios and estimating the entropy of a quantum system when its density matrix is unknown. A prototype of this new approach is presented, with sample complexity at a specific level of accuracy, although a more efficient variant is known to exist with a lower sample complexity. This new estimate of density matrix also finds uses in analyzing the efficiency of quantum state learning in specific scenarios and estimating the entropy of a quantum system when its density matrix is unknown.

The growth of AI is heavily reliant on advanced computing infrastructure, 
efficient data management, and smart utilization of cloud services to support 
the AI development cycle. Effective integration of high-performance computing 
(HPC) techniques, scalable data storage, and intelligent cloud usage plays a 
crucial role in accelerating AI development. In the realm of AI, the rapid 
accumulation of vast datasets necessitates refined data management strategies 
to enhance computational efficiency. Simultaneously, leveraging public and 
private cloud computing resources provides essential computing power for 
complex AI tasks, requiring careful load balancing and resource allocation. 
Finally, the AI development cycle itself demands streamlined development, 
testing, and deployment processes through continuous integration and 
automation, streamlined user interfaces, and comprehensive AI pipeline 
management tools.

This study proposes a novel semi-self-supervised framework for automatically categorizing diagnosis codes from unlabelled electronic medical records. The method employs contrastive learning in a memory bank to align representations of diagnoses from different sources, enhancing the model's ability to capture the semantic meaning of ICD-10 codes in medical narratives. The framework, named ICD-ASCA, consists of two key components: first, it uses a clinical note encoder to convert unstructured medical notes into a shared embedding space, and second, it integrates this embedding with diagnoses sampled from clinical narratives to create a contrastive learning framework. The framework's performance has been validated using a training dataset of 25,000 labelled ICD-10 diagnoses and 100,000 unlabelled clinical notes, and comparisons with state-of-the-art classifiers have demonstrated improved accuracy across 100 diagnostic categories.

Consider a polynomial ring $S=k[x_1,\ldots,x_s]$ in $s$ variables. A monomial ideal $I$ within this ring is nearly Cohen-Macaulay if its local cohomology modules $H^{i}_{\mathfrak{m}}(S/I)$ for $i<\dim S-I$ are all torsion. This paper provides specific conditions to determine the nearly Cohen-Macaulay property of a monomial ideal based on its associated primes. A related classification is provided for nearly equidimensional Gorenstein lattice polyhedral divisors, certain sublattices of a free abelian group, and equidimensional lattice divisors on a toric variety. Additionally, conditions on lattice ideals for being nearly Cohen-Macaulay are established.

Current progress in quantum technology allows for the creation of complex, interconnected quantum systems.  These systems exhibit unique behaviors, potentially allowing for the adaptation of novel algorithms to existing quantum devices.  From a quantum computing perspective, the primary objective is to build large-scale, fault-tolerant machines, whereas current quantum devices serve as valuable platforms for exploring fundamental physics and simulating complex processes.  Researchers have initially investigated various quantum machine learning approaches combining artificial neural networks with quantum circuits.  Although promising, these methods face limitations due to their classical aspects.  This paper presents a fully quantum-driven methodology, utilizing autonomous quantum circuits.  We demonstrate this method using a 16-qubit superconducting quantum processor and obtain unexpected classification results on the MNIST dataset.  Notably, our quantum algorithm outperforms a traditionally used classical neural network on the same task, leveraging the inherent quantum properties for improved performance.

The discovery rate of exoplanets outside our solar system is rapidly increasing thanks to large-scale photometric surveys, particularly the Korean Microlensing Telecope Network (KMTNet). Although numerous Kepler-like exoplanets are identified each year by KMTNet, current searches for microlensing exoplanets primarily rely on visual inspection, which is time-consuming and limits the overall efficiency. To expand the search for exoplanets to encompass all available data from the three Southern Hemisphere telescopes, we employed six different machine learning and anomaly detection methods to scan KMTNet data collected during prime-field surveys in 2018. A comprehensive dataset of 10,132 light curves was analyzed using this approach, yielding 14 potential exoplanet candidates that exhibited characteristic dips in brightness consistent with planet transits. The initial findings have narrowed down the candidates to 8 cases that will be the focus of in-depth investigation to confirm their status as exoplanets. The success of using these techniques has validated their effectiveness in detecting microlensing exoplanets and paves the way for applying them to search for more exoplanets using KMTNet data.

Modern real-time inverse problem solvers heavily rely on backpropagation's
adjoint method to obtain gradients for iteratively refining solutions.
Adjoint networks effectively reuse forward passes, reducing differentiable
parsing system sizes by nearly half. Nevertheless, current adjoins are
limited by the inability to differentiate complex operations like shadowing,
previously excluded from the design. In this study, we establish the rules for
differentiating shadows, develop an adjacent size-adjoint network in setup,
and demonstrate its benefits, reducing overall network size by two-thirds.

Recent research has successfully applied Bayesian methods to estimate transportation demand, but current techniques only provide point estimates requiring data from multiple days. This limits their practical use for cities that can't monitor origins and destinations over several days. To address this issue, a probabilistic model based on stochastic user equilibrium is developed, allowing estimation of transportation demand using data from just one day of a specific origin-destination period. A case study using data from New York City verifies the model, comparing its results with other methods, including Dynamic Average Path Cost and Maximum Likelihood Estimation, and demonstrating its practical value.

The oscillation patterns of various natural phenomena are often irregular and unpredictable due to their complex and diverse characteristics. Consequently, oscillation arrays in various systems, such as neural networks, may exhibit both synchronized and desynchronized behaviors. Our research focuses on a systematic analysis of zero-phase synchronization, highlighting its distinctions from other oscillation patterns. We propose an analytical framework based on the multiple-time scale method and verify the findings through numerical experiments. The outcomes of our studies reveal crucial factors influencing the synchronization dynamics, such as heterogeneity in oscillation frequencies and the distribution of parameters within the array. Our research provides a comprehensive method for investigating synchronization patterns in diverse systems with varying properties.

Two well-known algorithms by Aldous and Broder and Wilson utilize random walks to create a spanning tree of a graph in polynomial time. Broder's analysis revealed that these algorithms are equivalent in nature, while also establishing that the resulting tree is uniform in distribution. Interestingly, this equivalence holds true not only for the final output but also for the underlying random processes generating the trees. This relationship implies that, for any given time frame, the trees generated by both algorithms at that specific instance have a conditional distribution that remains unchanged. Leveraging this concept, we have developed a universal two-stage method to generate the desired uniform spanning trees.

This work introduces a new dataset, referred to as MusicTM, which comprises a collection of three sheets featuring music, lyrics, and corresponding audio recordings. The collection also includes audio files that showcase each sheet music piece both with and without piano accompaniment. Primarily, the collection consists of traditional Japanese songbook collections called Songbooks, for which there are 3 sheets available along with their audio versions. The MusicTM collection serves as a resource that facilitates simultaneous visual and auditory analysis. Its uniform structure enables concurrent visual and auditory feature extraction. Moreover, its simultaneous presentation of sheet music and audio enables side-by-side comparison and integration of these features. Lastly, its varying accompaniment forms enable exploration of content consistency across different versions. The research presents an initial approach utilizing this dataset.

A recent breakthrough in Natural Language Processing (NLP) has revolutionized our understanding of the relationships between different entities in language, through the development of word embeddings. By analyzing the linguistic context of each word, these embeddings enable the creation of a semantic map that places similar words in close proximity. This breakthrough has far-reaching implications for various applications, including dating historical events based on the publication dates of newspapers, identifying word meanings through spatial relationships, and exploring cultural associations. In contrast to supervised learning methods that require extensive datasets, unsupervised approaches can generate embeddings from vast repositories such as Wikidata, creating a unified knowledge base that facilitates visual exploration of the derived entity distributions.

The effects of a cubic nonlinearity and dispersion on dark soliton stability in a two-dimensional system are examined. Our research reveals how nonlinearity and dispersion influence dark soliton stability and positioning. We demonstrate that a cubic instability arises when the soliton has a specific refractive index, leading to collapse. Our analysis shows that a dark soliton in two dimensions is stable if its intensity follows a power law greater than one. We also found that a force from refractive index gradients keeps the soliton centered. We demonstrated that a higher exponent in the soliton's intensity profile delays the cubic instability and allows for greater soliton speed. We used numerical simulations to study the soliton's behavior during collapse and found that a profiled power in the refraction depends on the cubic collapse threshold.

This paper introduces a practical approach to directing users within a visual context.
We present 'Lotse', a modular framework that is both user-friendly and easy to integrate existing components.
Through hands-on demonstrations, a case study in Dark Matter Research, and discussions on its applicability to other domains, we explore how Lotse can be effectively utilized in various contexts. We also reflect on its limitations and potential areas for improvement.

These features make the stellarator a prime candidate for advanced plasma research.
